maintopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to conclude the few remarks I made last Friday when I was given the opportunity to speak on the problem of Canadian unity, I should like to suggest that it might be advisable, in spite of the polls conducted among others, by the members for Trois-Rivieres and Brome-Missisquoi (Messrs. Mongrain and Grafftey) to question the sociological value of those surveys, and to refrain from concluding categorically that separatism is not a threat in the province of Quebec for the simple reason that, in fact, it is not dangerous. There is nevertheless a separatist possibility which should be of concern and which might be combatted by a vigorous policy to consolidate Canadian unity.
May I, Mr. Speaker, suggest the following recommendations: first, I believe the government should take the initiative through the Canada Council or a department of cultural affairs, if there was one, of sending across the country the greatest names of the French-Canadian artistic community. They would certainly play a more important and a more effective role in promoting national unity than any election or political speech. I am sure for instance that Monique Leyrac would create a much deeper impression than any member giving out a patriotic speech. There should be an offensive whereby our artists would travel throughout the country to bring home the French fact within the framework of greater Canadian solidarity.
Secondly, I would suggest more frequent exchanges between all members from the province of Quebec sitting in this house. I know it has been tried before, particularly at the time of the Gordon affair, but election strategy is always taken into account. I should certainly favour having all members from the province of Quebec, notwithstanding their political affiliation-it is not quite what could be called a common front-holding more frequent exchanges to defend common interests.
Thirdly-this would bring a smile to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Trudeau) if he were here-I would support, Mr. Speaker, the initiative of the government or a subsidized organization calling not the
October 10, 19S7

Estates General of French Canada, but the Estates General of Canadian unity, that is to say, I am sure the Estates General of French Canada will have an important role to play and will produce interesting results. But I believe that, after this initiative with interesting results, it might be appropriate to call right across Canada, if I may use an expression of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), some kind of get-together of everyone concerned in consolidating Canadian unity, people picked all over, among social clubs, various bodies and various associations, somewhat along the lines of the Estates General of French Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is talk of a conference on language rights. This is also a most interesting initiative but, in my opinion, to say that French-speaking communities have the right to have a French school if they want one is no solution to the problem, which goes deeper. The real problem is that in a great part of Canada the French culture is as foreign as the Chinese or the Arab culture. The best solution is not to force a language or a culture on anyone, but to render French culture attractive to the majority of Canadians.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on the budget will be in an effort to try to put forward, as I have in the last two years, some ideas on the theory of budgeting which I think might be helpful to a minister of finance in trying to solve the problem of the high costs that assail our economy at the present time.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I am going to suggest at the outset that the time has come in Canada, and I suggest also in the United States, to do some serious thinking in connection with the basic doctrines that guide ministers of finance in budgeting. Since the late thirties the United States and

The Budget-Mr. Hamilton Canada have accepted the principle enunciated by Lord Keynes. In essence this is the principle that by the actions of governments the ups and downs of the economic cycle could be reduced. The efforts of governments in the western democracies to employ the teachings of Lord Keynes have been remarkably successful, but I submit that at this stage of our economic history the application of Lord Keynes' doctrine of either putting tremendous expansionist forces to work in times of recession or of putting deflationary forces to work in times of inflation ought to be reconsidered.
I put forward that suggestion not with any thought of posing as an expert in these matters but rather as a person who is trying to see his way through the dilemma facing a minister of finance who is attempting to run the government of Canada along what appears to him to be a highway. When the minister finds he is running downhill too fast he tries to put on the brakes; when he slows down going up the next hill he tries to speed up a little.
If we use the doctrines of Lord Keynes they are, in the first instance, not applicable to Canada in their complete form, and second I submit they are the wrong approach to take. First of all let me examine the major premises of Lord Keynes. He argued that by the use of taxation power and monetary practices the state could slow down the rising tide of inflation. And he was right. However, the thing to remember, Mr. Speaker, is that he designed his theory for the United Kingdom. His theory was designed to meet the needs of a country that is completely homogeneous, a country which is very sophisticated in its industry, a country which is an importer of raw materials, a country which is an exporter of finished goods, a country which over most of its economic history has had a surplus in external account and, as a result, is thereby able to export capital.
Let us contrast the country for which Lord Keynes developed his theory, Mr. Speaker, with Canada. We find that obviously Canada is not an homogeneous country. Canada is a country of at least 12 if not 15 districts each with an economy different from that of any other section of the country. Second, Canada is not completely sophisticated in its industrial activities. We have a range from the very beginning of an industry up to industries which have been established for a long time and are able to compete world wide. In other words we have a great range of sophistication in our industry. Third, Mr. Speaker,
2928	-	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton Canada is not an importer of raw materials; it is an exporter of raw materials. Fourth, Canada is an importer of finished goods. And finally we usually have a negative balance in external account, which means that we have to import capital to keep our expansion moving. This is quite proper.
I contend that on the strength of these five distinct differences alone there is reason to re-examine the application of the Keynesian doctrine to Canadian economics.
I intimated in my first sentence or so, Mr. Speaker, that I thought the same situation should prevail in the case of the United States, and I now come back to deal with that suggestion. There has been a great deal of thought about, and writing devoted to, this particular subject. One of the first moves made in Canada in this regard was the setting up of the Porter royal commission, which reported in 1964. A reading of chapter 20 of that report makes it very clear that the commissioners recognized that the application of monetary policy in Canada, separated as it was from fiscal policy, was ruinous to governments that have held office in this country. It ruined the St. Laurent government economically; it certainly ruined us, and I suspect that at times it has come close to ruining the present minister, as indicated last September when he came in with his baby budget.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is apparent that those in Canada who have devoted their attention to this question have come up with the concept that something is wrong with the application of the doctrine of Lord Keynes. Since the Porter commission reported I think it is fair to say that our monetary policy and our fiscal policy have been co-ordinated in a much better way. As a matter of fact, with the change of the governor in 1961 there began to be a better synchronization of monetary and fiscal policy, and I cite that as one piece of evidence in support of my contention. The subject I am talking about now is not new to me or in any way original.
The second matter I should like to recall to the memory of the house is the second annual review of the Economic Council of Canada for December, 1965. This review was directed toward achieving a sustained and balanced economic growth. The whole volume deals with the suggestions of the Economic Council of Canada on how to face the fact that Canada is a country of regions; that within those regions there is great disparity of income, great disparity of education, and tremendous disparity of opportunity.

DEBATES	October 10, 1967
The council suggested, as well as it could make suggestions in such a general type of volume, that government policy together with monetary and fiscal policy should be directed toward this regional character of Canada. At the end of the volume the council made certain recommendations, but I have seen evidence of only one of those suggestions in the budget that we have before us.
More fascinating still, Mr. Speaker, is the book which was published last December written by Walter Heller, the gentleman who served under President Kennedy and President Johnson as head of the council of economic advisers to the president. This book is called "New Dimensions of Political Economy" and it reached Canadian book stores last December. In this volume Walter Heller discusses the question of timing; of how governments are failing to apply the principles of Lord Keynes by not being able to move fast enough for various reasons.
I am not going to go into the detail of the various reasons governments are slow to move. In some states, because of the slowness of getting legislation through congress it is a very difficult task to give the executive power to move. We in Canada have a better system, Mr. Speaker. If the Minister of Finance asked us to give him certain powers to move either backward or forward, or sideways for that matter, then he would be given the power to move to the extent that statistics indicated that the country's policies should change direction.
I am aware that the minister is fully knowledgeable of this, and I congratulate him for showing an awareness that there is a weakness in the type of budgeting that governments in Canada adopt. However, in his budget speech last June he suggested that he was not yet ready to ask parliament to grant him this type of power. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the time has now come, and that in the next budget the house should be asked by the Minister of Finance-if he is a responsible minister-to give him the power to move, with timing suited to the need, so as to check the economy by, if necessary, slowing it down in any particular sector.
This brings me, Mr. Speaker, to my main point. So far I have suggested that the timing in the application of the techniques of controlling the economy has to be improved in Canada. Therefore I suggest that the timing of government action should not be made retroactive; that in future power be given the minister in our budget legislation to make moves either backward or forward in the
October 10, 1967	COMMONS
same fiscal year; and further, that if parliament is equally responsible it should grant the minister those powers.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, I am suggesting that we know enough now about controlling the economy through the actions of government that we can trust to the ability of those who are guiding the minister to use the appropriate measures quickly and effectively-if they can be stopped and started -particularly if industry knows in advance what the measures might be. This is why they have to be listed in budget legislation.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
From close study of this question it is apparent that timing alone is not enough. Last year in my budget speech I suggested that we had to add a second principle to the doctrine of Lord Keynes. It is not a contradiction of Lord Keynes but a refinement of his doctrine, and is designed to meet the problems of regional development in Canada as well as the varying range of our industries in their sophistication and maturity. In my budget debate speech of April 29, 1965, I warned the minister of inflationary pressures, listing some of them, and I suggested some short and long term proposals. Nevertheless the budget of April, 1965, was an inflationary budget when the signs of inflation were there for all to see. That was a clear example of how the minister, instead of checking inflation after it had begun, fed gasoline to the flames.
That was in 1965. By February and March, 1966, it was clear that the economy was overheating. The overheating of 1965 and 1966 reached its peak in February and March of 1966, and almost all indicators showed that a decline was setting in. Yet two months later the minister brought in a budget that put on the brakes.
Here one sees that the economy was accelerating toward inflation and the minister added fuel to the flames; when the inflation had built up and turned down, he put on the brakes. The timing was out by almost 12 months. By the minister having made these mistakes in timing an argument could be made out to show that the government has failed to heed the warnings of a collection of statistics which show instantly what every indicator is doing. The public ought to know of these indicators, because were they heeded, before it became too late, we ought to be able to tell instantly when the economy begins to falter. There are 15 or 16 indicators.
DEBATES	2929
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton
Let me continue the unhappy story. In June of 1967 the minister brought in a program of heavy government spending. That was definitely an inflationary budget. This June, after the indicators had pointed steadily downward since March of 1966, he concluded that there was need for an inflationary budget and brought in an inflationary budget, just as the indicator had moved up again. Once again he was one year out of date. We are now told that the government is heavily pruning expenditures.
It is easy for those on this side of the house to condemn the minister for being one year too late. Really he suffers from not having a definite philosophy; he is not sure of the type of budget to bring down with the tools he has at hand. The emphasis now surely is on the need for better statistical information. The emphasis surely ought to be on giving the Minister of Finance a long range growth target. The evidence is surely clear that the means through which the minister may take instant action must be at his fingertips at all times.
I am suggesting, therefore, as my first major point that the timing procedure with respect to these matters must be improved in Canada. The way to do that is to give the minister certain powers. Many suggestions have been put forward. Certain powers could be given to him annually, for one year at a time, and they could be renewed as the house saw fit.
My second proposal, as I said earlier, has to do with selectivity. To project a picture that one may visualize, I suggest the Minister of Finance sitting behind the wheel of a car. This is what he does, too. As he is going downhill he sees a few icy patches ahead so he applies the brakes gently; but then he sees a hill and accelerates, and it is that vision he has in his mind when he thinks of a budget.
I suggest that because of the unusual nature of our country he should visualize himself as walking a tightrope. This tightrope is fixed; it undulates to a certain extent, yes, but the danger is that if he falls off to one side or the other he will fall into deflation or inflation. I suggest that is because Canada is a broken type of country, made up of regions. One region may have tremendous inflationary pressures such as we have seen these last two or three years in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal; and if one were to think that all Canada is affected as these cities are the minister would be tempted to put on the brakes, clamp on the controls and slow down spending.
2930	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton
As he does that, though, there are dozens of other districts throughout the country-rural British Columbia, Abitibi in Quebec, Lac St. Jean in Quebec, Gaspe, the whole of the maritimes and the greater part of northern Ontario-which suffer from a surplus of manpower, a surplus of productive capacity. Are the brakes to be put on for those areas, too?
I described the last budget speech as a castor oil treatment. Three people out of 15 are sick, yet each of the 15 has to take castor oil. The minister must realize that fundamentally Canada is made up of a number of different regions, and where there is a need to put the brakes on for one area to hold down its costs, there is a need to add coal to another to enable it to gain speed. In the long run the cure for inflation is to cure its basic cause, which is lack of productivity. Increasing productivity, making sure that human and material resources are being fully utilized, in the long run is the best guarantee against inflation.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? In the opinion of the hon. member has inflation pretty well run its course? Ought we to be preparing deflationary policies?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In answering that question let me say that I am trying to outline for the hon. member the weakness of acting after the horse has left the barn. I am suggesting that at this stage the Minister of Finance is too late; the fuel has been poured on the fire. Nevertheless he should be doing several different things. If inflationary pressures affect two or three areas, that is no reason this coming spring to clamp a tight money policy on us all and slow down the entire country. I shall come to that in a minute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member a
question? I find his speech most interesting. I wish to know what his indicators, that he has access to, now indicate for the future.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Department of Trade and Commerce, which the minister once headed, publishes reports every month giving the various indicators. If one looks at the indicators for 1966 one will see that 15 or 16 are listed. These indicators show that the economy started turning down in February or March. I did not bring the data with me; I am trying to make a general speech on principle.
Returning to the question of selectivity, I suggest that it must apply to the monetary

DEBATES	October 10, 1967
and fiscal sides simultaneously. The question to be asked here and now is, how can this be done? That is what I shall wind up with. I have said clearly and I hope emphatically that timing alone is not enough. There must be selectivity by regions and by industries. By regions, I think it has been indicated, one can clearly define an economic area.
I have seen tangible evidence within these last three or four years of what I talk about. Within a few miles of Montreal one finds an almost complete recession; if one goes through the towns of northern Ontario at this very moment one will see, when we are suffering from inflation in some cities, that there is unused manpower and unused capacity. It appears to me, therefore, beyond question that there is merit in trying to visualize monetary policy as applied to regions.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Let me turn now to a consideration of the effects of monetary and fiscal policy applied to industry. It is evident there are certain industries in Canada which have demonstrated year by year since 1961 that they possess competitive advantages over industries in other parts of the world, for example, in the United States. I gave one example the other day when I referred to the steel industry which was being hard pressed to meet the demands placed on it. This situation has since been corrected and steel has moved into a surplus position. I maintain that when we enjoy an advantage of this kind we in Canada should do everything possible to build up certain industries, not by imposing artificial restrictions at the border but by positive techniques using the laws of economics. The way to hurt such industries is to impose monetary restrictions making it difficult for them to gather the capital they need in order to expand.
It would seem wise, therefore, to select certain industries which are in the position of enjoying a comparative advantage and make sure we apply our fiscal and monetary policy on a selective basis so as to enable them to get still farther ahead. How could this be done? Well, we have the machinery at hand; it has been available to us all along. As a clue I intend to read a dispatch from Washington which appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 6, 1966. The headline reads: "Make Loans Selective, Fowler Tells Banks".
Treasury Secretary Fowler yesterday urged banks to turn down or scale back the less deserving loan applications to help prevent an inflationary boom.
October 10, 1967

It's important, he said, that the turn to moderation in the growth of bank credit be accomplished without skyrocketing of interest rates.
How far seeing he was.
Raising the price of money, he asserted, "should not

and need not-be the only means of determining which applicants get the loans."
I could read further to illustrate the way in which Mr. Fowler is suggesting to the United States banks-and there are hundreds of thousands of them-that they should take on the job of being selective in the credit they allow.
What about Canada? We do not have thousands of banks; in fact, we have fewer than ten. The banks have always professed a desire to participate in carrying out monetary policy. We well remember the clashes which have taken place between the banks and the Bank of Canada over the years. If the banks want a chance to help carry out fiscal policy there is an obvious way in which they can do so. Suppose, for example, there were heavy inflationary pressures in the big cities of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver and it was thought wise to impose a curb. It would be of very little use to cut down the total number of loans made across Canada by, say, 10 per cent because 90 per cent of the loans made would still go to the big cities, leaving even less in all probability for the marginal areas. If there really were a desire to restrict the amount of credit from the big cities this could be brought about by making a serious reduction in the amounts of money placed at the disposal of those cities. Such a step might in turn encourage the banks to make more money available in the marginal areas.
AH I know is that nothing of this kind is being done at the present time and there is no harm in trying. It could be done by zones. The machinery is there. Canada at this moment is not in any danger economically, I would suggest. The danger arises from our lack of ability to guide the system.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this our centennial year all of us are proud to be Canadians. We have, I believe, wrought a miracle out of a "few acres of snow", as Voltaire once described Canadian colonies.
In the space of a short 100 years, hardly a moment in the history of America and a mere speck of time in the larger history of humankind, we have wrought a nation that stands second on this earth in the only important task, that of providing a better life for all its people. This is the only criterion by which we may ultimately judge a political entity, as illustrated in Rousseau's famous utterance that "all the world is people and what is not people is not worth the counting".
More remarkable stiH is the fact that in doing this we have won the respect of all the people on the earth. We have played a role in the councils of the world which has been far beyond our numbers and political power. In both war and peace we have discharged our international obligations with the same amazing capacity that we have applied to our domestic ones.
Of all this we may and should be justly proud, and in our centennial year we Canadians have had the opportunity to pause and examine these wonders so that we could truly realize our national potential in the light of our proud beginnings. Our future greatness will come from nowhere but from within ourselves.
On this hundredth anniversary of our confederation I am also proud to be a Liberal and a member of this government. Our leader has been largely responsible for the respect we enjoy in the world community. After five years under this government the economy is strong and employment is at its highest level in the history of our country. Unemployment is low-this may be attested by the premier of Ontario who goes about the province boasting about how low it is-largely as a result of the federal government's efforts. The problems we face today are generally problems of affluence, not of depression. The problems we face are those of maintaining prosperity while preventing the overheating of our economy resulting in high prices and high wages.
The government and the country are in a strong financial position and we intend to keep it that way. There will be no repetition of the 1962 crisis which occurred under the
2932	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Benson last Tory government. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) set out as our aim in 1968-69 a balanced budget on a national accounts basis and the government intends to achieve this.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: THE BUDGET

The federal government of Canada is the biggest business in our country and it needs to be run as such. Government expenditures are always a source of worry, and so they should be in many areas. The Economic Council of Canada in its fourth annual review urged the need to develop procedures for controlling the size and structure of federal government expenditures. I do not for a moment deprecate the competence and wisdom of the members of the Economic Council but I wish to take this occasion to point out to the house that in the past four years the government has taken very positive steps in the direction indicated by the council. Indeed, at the present time the government of Canada in many ways leads other governments throughout the world in the development of sophisticated new methods to ensure that every cent of the taxpayers' dollar yields optimum advantages to this country.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
A few days ago my colleague, the Minister of Finance, pointed out the dangers of inflation, that the government's objective for the next fiscal year is to reduce the budget deficit substantially below the level of the current fiscal year, and what strong and positive steps had already been taken to reduce federal expenditures. I join with my colleague in his concern but I also wish to bring to the attention of hon. members in the course of this speech that these reductions will be made on a consistent basis. Reductions in every major department of government have taken place under our budget exercise for 1968-69.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some programs which the government has undertaken cannot be measured in pure financial terms. These include programs such as family allowances, supplementary old age pensions, the Canada Assistance Plan, health insurance, and medicare which is to be introduced in 1968, all programs of Liberal governments. These are programs for people and they must be continued by this government. After all, we are a Liberal government and our first priority is to look after the ordinary people of this country.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are other programs which cannot be curtailed, programs that are essential in dealing with the particular problems of regional growth. These are programs such as manpower retraining, ARDA, the Atlantic Development Board, and the area development program. These must be proceeded with no matter what else the government may have to do.
The house should recall that out of the current budget of $9j billion almost 50 per cent of the total budget falls into a category of expenditures which are required by statute or which represent long-term commitments to international organizations of which Canada is a member. Of this percentage over two thirds represents public debt charges, direct payments to other levels of government, hospital insurance and family and youth allowances. As an example I might state that because of population growth the increase in hospitalization costs in the past five years has been in excess of $150 million, and the increase in family allowances because of the growth in our population over the same period has amounted to almost $90 million. Employment stimulation and price support for agricultural products represent another significant percentage.
There remains, then, some $4 billion over which the government can exercise more direct control. This afternoon I would like to report to the house on what the Treasury Board has done and is planning to do in this area, but first I think it appropriate to place these very important matters in their historical perspective.
October 10, 1967

It will be recalled that when the Glassco commission recognized the need to strengthen government control over expenditures the prime organizational recommendation was the separation of the Treasury Board from the Department of Finance, including the creation of a new portfolio, the President of the Treasury Board.
On January 20, 1964, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) announced that the government had approved these proposals and intended to proceed with appropriate legislation. On February 3, 1964, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) was appointed President of the Privy Council and vice chairman of the Treasury Board so that he could begin implementation of this phase of the Glassco commission recommendations. In May of the same year, Dr. George Davidson, who had been a senior deputy minister for more than 15 years and more recently director of the bureau of government organization, was appointed secretary of the Treasury Board. On December 18, 1965, the Prime Minister appointed me to succeed the Minister of Public Works as vice chairman of the Treasury Board, and on October 3, 1966, when parliament approved the Government Organization Act I had the honour of being appointed the first President of the Treasury Board. With these changes we were in a position to begin the development of the role of the Treasury Board as manager of the public service and to upgrade federal government management firmly along the lines recommended by the Glassco commission.
In 1962 the Glassco commission in its report on financial management made an extensive set of recommendations designed to provide more effective departmental control of existing operations, improved governmental assessment and control of both new and existing programs, and more complete and meaningful information on public expenditures to parliament.
In the summer of 1963, as a result of Treasury Board urging, four departments hired consultants to test the efficacy of the Glassco proposals aimed at improved departmental control of operations. The consultants were also instructed to recommend a detailed plan of implementation. Following a favourable report from these consultants the Treasury Board authorized the four departments, Transport, Agriculture, Northern Affairs and National Resources, and Veterans Affairs to implement the consultants' recommendations. Later, as a result of further
The Budget-Mr. Benson Treasury Board urging, additional departments began the introduction of these modern financial management techniques.
As a means of assisting departments in this work the Treasury Board in 1964 authorized the comptroller of the treasury to create a consulting group known as "Accounting Advisory Services," and in 1965 we were in a position to authorize to certain key departments the issue of a preliminary version of a guide on financial management. In 1966 we approved the issue of all departments and agencies of the government of Canada of a final version of this comprehensive guide. We are proud to have been associated with this guide which has received international acclaim.
The new emphasis that we in the Treasury Board have placed on improved control by departments over operations has led to the appointment of a number of senior comptrollers from prviate industry to positions of chief finance officer in departments, and has resulted in an extensive training program in financial management in the government service carried out in co-operation with the professional accounting societies.
I think that all members of this house should be aware that as a result of the financial management improvement program which is now in its fourth year a majority of the departments and agencies are concentrating on a drive toward improving the management control of existing operations, and that the Treasury Board is gaining access to more meaningful data to exercise its central managerial role.
I might add that the Treasury Board is giving active consideration to proposing to parliament further amendments to the Financial Administration Act. These amendments would, in a phased and orderly fashion, shift certain responsibilities for pre-audit and commitment control of government expenditures from the comptroller of the treasury to the various departments of government. Should these amendments be approved by parliament it will mean that the government has implemented all the important recommendations made by the Glassco commission in its report on financial management. In this regard I would invite hon. members opposite and the public accounts committee to inquire concerning progress on specific recommendations made by the Glassco commission, and I repeat that we will have implemented all the major recommendations of that commission.
2934	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Benson
We in the Treasury Board appreciate that while financial management has promoted and will promote more effective control over operations in the departments, it will not in itself solve the basic problem of how to make the best use of scarce and costly resources. With this in mind we began at an early date to take a positive interest in what is known as program budgeting and how this important new concept could be applied to the circumstances of the Canadian government.
Program budgeting is concerned with the presentation of expenditure proposals in a way that will enable effective decisions to be made on the allocation of necessarily scarce resources. This approach concentrates on objectives and benefits rather than solely on conventional elements such as cost. Furthermore, it emphasizes longer term dollar requirements rather than just those of the next year, and requires that consideration be given to indirect and associated costs as well as those directly related to a given proposal. Program budgeting is, therefore, a device to bring together related proposals from different departments so that a more complete picture can be presented. Furthermore, using this approach in every appropriate instance, proposals would be subjected to systematic analysis both as to objectives and as to alternative ways to achieve these objectives.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The United States government had pioneered in the development of these techniques and therefore this government sent a group of senior officials to Washington for discussions with the United States bureau of the budget. At that time it was found that program budgeting was being applied only in the United States department of defence. However, the Treasury Board decided to introduce program budgeting concurrently in both the civil and defence departments of the government of Canada.
We have already progressed far toward this goal. A new form of the estimates, which was recommended by consultants hired for this purpose, has been drafted and was approved by the Treasury Board in early 1966. It will provide parliament with a far more meaningful picture of departmental spending estimates in that it describes activities in which departments are engaged and the program objectives which these activities are meant to serve. In other words, it is designed to measure the advisability of expenditures from a benefit point of view as well as their legality.

DEBATES	October 10, 1967
Unfortunately, in spite of repeated attempts it has not yet been possible to lay this new form of the estimates before the public accounts committee of the house for its consideration. For this reason, all estimates will be formally presented to parliament this year in the traditional blue book and according to the traditional form so long as parliament desires. However, the Treasury Board is continuing its new line of development and a separate printing of the estimates in the new form, as separate booklets, will be prepared for 26 departments. These booklets will be laid before the parliamentary committees concerned with these departments at the time when the departments' estimates come under committee review.
The house will appreciate that these new concepts of financial management and program budgeting require a much improved system for the planning and recording of expenditures. Such a system has now been created. It provides for the coding of expenditures according to programs and activities and an internal departmental responsibility structure. We are confident that this new uniform system will also better serve the needs of economic analysis. We look forward to an early opportunity to explain this coding system and the new form of the estimates to the public accounts committee.
Forecasting is an essential feature of effective program budgeting. All members know that many proposed expenditures affect not only the current year but in some cases many years to come. In 1962 departments were required to present, in conjunction with their estimates for the fiscal year 1963-64, a multiyear forecast on a vote basis. In 1964, as a result of the urging of the then minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon)-and I might add for the first time in the history of the government of Canada-departmental expenditure targets were set by the Treasury Board against which each department could carry out its estimates' preparation.
One of the consultants had recommended the separation of the consideration of the multi-year forecast from that of the new year forecast. This made sense, and in 1965 the submission and consideration of the multiyear forecast was moved to the spring so that targets to be set could be derived from these forecasts after due consideration by the Treasury Board and cabinet. This represented the first major step toward a fullfledged program review. In 1966 seven departments cooperated in presenting their estimates in the
October 10, 19S7

new form whereby operations were shown in large segments called "programs", made up in turn of smaller related segments called "activities". In 1967 about 20 additional departments presented their program proposals in this new form. Review of these and the conventional forecasts of the remaining departments led to a recommendation to cabinet and the recent setting of targets by cabinet for the year 1968-69. I might add that this greatly facilitated the recent cuts in expenditures for 1968-69.
From what I have said so far hon. members will recognize that the Treasury Board and cabinet have so far concentrated on the forthcoming fiscal year. The program review documents included projections of expenditure levels for the next five years, and the departments not yet following the new form were required to present similar projections. I intend, however, that following the consideration of detailed estimates this fall the staff of the Treasury Board will examine the revised expenditure proposals and forecasts that the departments have submitted for the next four years. Taking into account the projections from the Department of Finance as to what funds are likely to be available, the staff of the Treasury Board will recommend the constraints within which each department should be instructed to formally plan for subsequent years. This will result in a further improvement in departmental plans since they will be, in effect, forced to establish priorities and to make recommendations as to what are the more essential needs.
The Treasury Board recognized that improved planning by departments would result in an increased necessity for choice at the governmental level even though departmental proposals would have been subjected to much deeper analysis, and further noted that expenditure proposals would continue to exceed the capacity of the economy to provide the necessarily scarce resources. However, the board also recognized that in the making of choices at the cabinet level a whole new range of techniques and technology was available which could be brought to bear in assisting in analysing such choices.
Accordingly, in March of 1966 we authorized the creation of a new division within the management improvement branch of the Treasury Board staff to be known as SIM-PAC, for "System of Integrated Management Planning and Control". These acronyms are very handy verbal shorthand but I must say I find them puzzling until they are explained
The Budget-Mr. Benson and then I am annoyed with myself for not having got the message immediately.
The SIMP AC division has been staffed with highly trained specialists in such management disciplines as computer technology, operations research, economics, accounting, and program budgeting. The division was instructed to design a fundamentally new system of planning and control of the kind referred to recently by the Economic Council of Canada.
As a result of co-operative efforts between the SIMPAC division and the divisions of the program branch of the Treasury Board, some of the general outlines of a modern system are beginning to emerge. I have already referred briefly to one of these. This is the necessity to forecast expenditures two, three, or four years in advance. As hon. members are aware, the government apparatus includes a large number of departments and agencies, many of whose responsibilities are interrelated. This means that future plans must be considered in terms of broad government objectives or functions rather than according to the narrow and perhaps parochial interests of individual departments or agencies. With this in mind the SIMPAC division has developed a functional classification of expenditures. One effect of this classification will be to draw together, from whatever department they are located in, the expenditures proposed for all related activities. The house will appreciate that this new classification will serve, far better than its predecessors, the analysis of alternative future patterns of expenditures.
Following this general theme it is proposed to develop in the Treasury Board secretariat a competence in what is known as "cost-benefit analysis". This will serve a variety of important purposes. In the first place, a searching review of departmental expenditure proposals on the part of the Treasury Board secretariat will stimulate improved analysis by departmental stags. Second, the central position of the Treasury Board will provide a better point of vantage for laying before ministers the full government-wide implications of departmental proposals. Third, by bringing analysis to bear on current and long-existing government activities, it will be possible to determine whether their continuation should be questioned by the government.
The Treasury Board stag is at present preparing a manual on program budgeting. This manual will emphasize the kind of analysis the departments will be expected to provide in support of their expenditure proposals.
October 10, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Benson The Treasury Board has also jointed with the department of manpower to make a full-scale analysis of a major activity in government. The findings of this analysis are expected not only to provide the department and the Treasury Board staff with first hand experience with these analytical techniques but also to provide illustrative material of the concepts the new manual will promote.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Program budgeting will rely for much of its success on the expansion of the sources of data on which planning will be based. As a result ministers will have much more data to consider in arriving at decisions. The most significant data contained in departmental program proposals is, therefore, being converted to a form suitable for processing by computers to permit presentation to ministers of the more relevant data in summarized and analysed form. This kind of data available for processing in this way will increase as it becomes available and as a better appreciation of computers for this purpose is gained. Advances in computer technology give promise of the very definite possibility within a very few years to respond more quickly to ministers' requests for analysis of a quite complex kind needed in arriving at decisions, and this government has every intention of taking full advantage of this new technology.
I might indicate that in the budget year 1969-70 those planning the budget will be able, I hope, to sit in a room and ask questions regarding what will be the effect of altering a particular program. We will be able to feed this information into a computer immediately and the data will be returned to indicate how many people will be affected, where they are located, what their income is and other relevant facts. Governments in the future will be in a much better position immediately to plan changes in programs and consider their effects based on an over-all view of government expenditures rather than the expenditures of a particular department or agency.
I mentioned earlier that the new draft form of the estimates will reflect a program activity structure rather than the traditional objects of expenditures. Parliament and cabinet will therefore tend to look upon the activities of departments as areas for review and the activity structure of programs is therefore of cardinal importance. It is the responsibility of the Treasury Board to approve the activity structure of each department on the basis that each activity is the appropriate aggregate for departmental planning and analysis

and the appropriate aggregate for ministerial and parliamentary review.
If I had had the time this afternoon I intended to say a few words about the staff of the civil service, since this question has been raised several times by hon. members opposite. Due to time consideration I shall choose a later opportunity to explain in detail the changes in the staff of the civil service. One thing I think all of us should bear in mind is that much of the staff of the civil service of Canada is service staff. For example, in looking at the 1968-69 plans for expansion of personnel the largest single expansion by far will be in the Post Office Department. The Post Office Department is a service department expected to provide service to the people of Canada. Our economy is becoming more and more an urban economy. Therefore we require more and more people to deliver mail to people in the urban communities. We also have the Montpetit report which suggests we should get rid of many casual personnel in the Post Office Department and replace them by permanent personnel. This is being done.
Another step that is being taken relates to the fact that in some large urban areas the Post Office Department is finding it more economical to take over its own transportation of mail rather than letting it out on contract. In doing this on a pilot project it has been proven that a great deal of money can be saved, but it requires more personnel in the Post Office Department. The mere fact there are more people working in the Post Office Department does not mean in this particular case that it costs the people of Canada more money. I will give detailed explanations of changes in personnel in the civil service at some subsequent opportunity.
At this point, however, I should like to point out that I do not personally believe in the freezing of civil service personnel. We must establish objectives and we must be willing to shift personnel from one program to another. The mere freezing of personnel, as was experienced under the previous government, is not the way to control growth of the civil service. We must look at the establishment to make sure that every individual within that establishment of the civil service is required in order to carry out the business to be done for the benefit of the Canadian people.
As my time is running out, I submit in conclusion that the Treasury Board has not been unaware of nor, indeed, unresponsive to the problems and responsibilities with which
October 10, 1967	COMMONS
it has been confronted. Much has been accomplished in the past four years and with this firm foundation now in place even more will be accomplished by this government in the years to come.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must begin by saying that I was impressed by the speech of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson). I cannot, however, like King Agrippa, say that I was almost persuaded, because I was not.

I suppose I was not "almost persuaded" because I made the mistake of reading such documents as the report of the Economic Council of Canada, the Auditor General's report, statistics derived from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the opinions of great, leading economists and the experiences of prominent businessmen. I was also able to hear the cries of the homeless of this country and to note some of the anxiety of those who are sensitized to present economic conditions. Apart from that, the minister's speech was an interesting effort, but although he pointed out what the government would be doing, all his grandiloquent phrases do not put these things into effect.
I like these general debates on the budget and the Speech from the Throne. There are some superficial observers of our parliamentary institution who think that unless we are dealing with legislation we are wasting time. It seems to me that they overlook the essence of the parliamentary system. They forget that we in an elected house are more than a mere legislative mill. Indeed, I think that a great deal of the trouble we have been getting into in recent years comes from the mass of massive legislation we have been trying to grind out. This, of course, stems from the proliferation of elections, which always produce a proliferation of promises. Many of these promises are in areas of provincial jurisdiction and that compounds the difficulty when we seek to deal with them in this house.
I am not a violent partisan. It is not that I have terrible difficulty in deciding how to vote on election day, but I do not derive any emotional satisfaction from criticizing those who belong to other parties.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps, however, this is a handicap, because in the last four years the government has given a multitude of opportunities for criticism even to such a gentle, dove-like person as myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, let yourself go.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is depressing that in a country so richly endowed as ours, that in a period which has so many of the ingredients of prosperity and progress, we should be faced in this budget debate and at this time in our history with problems of grave and serious proportions in our economic sector. We seem destined to close our centennial celebration not with a great whoop of joy but with feelings of anxiety and uncertainty in the economic field and, let us face it, in other fields as well. For some of these difficulties, of course, we cannot hold the government responsible. Some factors are beyond its control or are perhaps even beyond the country's control. We recognize this, but as many of my colleagues have pointed out, a very serious indictment can be laid against this government.
We cannot say that this situation exists because of factors over which we have no control. The economists in my university days used to use the old expression that when the United States sneezes the whole world gets a cold. But today, as we look at comparative statistics, we seem to be shivering in many areas in which the United States is showing all the signs of health.
If there is one comment-and despite the invitation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), I am not going to be critical-which might be made about the present government, it would be that I have observed over the last four years its inability ever to anticipate anything. So many times the government seems to be overwhelmed and terribly surprised at the results of its own actions or inactions. As the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) said the other night, its leadership is shown by the frequency with which it tends to back into situations.
Many specifics have been charged against the government. Many interesting comments have been made on specific economic programs. I was going to talk about some of the recommendations of the Auditor General's report in reference to the Glassco commission. I noted what the minister said about the major recommendations. I cannot find in the
October 10, 1967	COMMONS
Auditor General's report a distinction between major and minor recommendations, and some time later in the session, perhaps through the order paper, I may elicit from the minister exactly how many of the 15 recommendations not disposed of according to the Auditor General's last report have in fact been implemented in this effort toward greater efficiency.
The matters with which the Auditor General dealt are important. We live in an era of big government. We know that. But surely we can ask that government departments set an example in efficiency. Time and money should be utilized in the best manner possible. In passing, Mr. Speaker, I must return to one of my frequent comments about the efficiency of our own chamber. For a number of years I have been appalled at the endless hours we in this house consume in waiting for votes to be taken and then for the calling and recording of those votes. A few days ago we had a scheduled evening sitting of two hours' length. Of those two hours we spent an hour and four minutes waiting for votes or having them recorded. Surely in the electronic age we can do a little better job on our one hundredth birthday in streamlining that time-consuming procedure.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: An electronic voting machine would compute the vote in seconds, and it should not be beyond the wisdom of the authorities to abandon that tedious, long process of waiting for votes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would an electronic system get the members here?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should think that on all votes except those which determine the fate of a government, and they should only be scheduled votes, the vote should be taken on the spot, because the other votes in essence deal with the procedure of the house. I have seen no system anywhere that is so archaic as ours. Having said this for the fifteenth time since I came here, I will now pass on to something else.
In this country, we are facing major economic problems on our one hundredth birthday. The Minister of Finance has been hearing about them. But I think we also have other, fundamental questions as we begin our second century. Our political life has taken on new dimensions and political questions carry with them a new degree of seriousness. It is not enough any more to ask which party 27053-1861
DEBATES	2939
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie will be the better or the best or what policies they will put into effect. In 1967 we must look not at policies or at personnel alone but, indeed, at the very type and structure of the country which any party or government must try to govern. Perhaps far reaching constitutional changes are necessary as we begin our second century. Possibly alterations less drastic and dramatic may be found preferable. But we must re-examine the basic constitutional structure and review longstanding practices and procedures in light of 1967 and post-1967 conditions.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Interestingly enough, Mr. Speaker, I believe the same opportunity, indeed the same compulsion, exists beyond the domestic field. I believe that for many reasons which lie beyond our own control we should reappraise our international role and position in the world. I believe we have passed the period of easy acceptance of traditional responsibilities and functions in the international scene. Some of the established organizations on which we have founded so much of our foreign policy are themselves in phases of transition or at least of reappraisal.
The United Nations has greatly changed since its establishment in 1945. Thoughtful people are concerned about its efficiency. They wonder about the peace keeping techniques, whether the peace restoring mechanisms are working well, or if in fact they are working at all. To cite one example, how long can we go on maintaining an uneasy peace in Cyprus if no ground has been made at all in the matter of conciliation?
We are also troubled about the financing of the United Nations. Article 109 of the charter speaks of revision; yet the world body has never been able to move in the direction of meaningful revision of its own structure. I believe that Canada as a charter member of the UN, and as a good member of the UN in contrast with our membership in the League of Nations, should, indeed must, seek to find whether there is an initiative it can take toward improving the structure of that world body.
NATO, another of our fundamental cornerstones, has changed greatly since 1947. Revision here may be necessary. Can it ever be the same after what has happened in the case of France? Are we attuned to the vast and bewildering changes in military science and strategy? Should the alliance extend and intensify its co-operation in the non-military field and diminish it in the military area?
October 10, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie Perhaps changes should be minimal, perhaps they should be fundamental; but let us look at the matter with high seriousness, and indeed with high priority.
Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) was asked a question today about NORAD. I am not a military expert, Mr. Speaker, far from it, and perhaps this should be my invitation to discuss the subject. For I am genuinely disquieted when reading about and hearing those who are experts deal with this question. Some of these experts suggest that the NORAD agreement has outlived its usefulness. Surely this is a fundamental question in the defence of our country. Should Canada opt out of this system? Should we accept the argument that because our contribution must necessarily be so small relative to that of the United States we should therefore totally disengage and follow other pursuits by directing our energies elsewhere?
There are those who argue that no matter what the state of technological advance, no matter what the preponderance of power on the side of our major ally, no self-respecting country like Canada can leave its defence totally to the people of another country. They argue that this country must offer more than geography to the defence of this continent, of which we occupy a large and somewhat vulnerable area. So here is another question, Mr. Speaker, which requires our earnest consideration, and I think requires it now.
I think the commonwealth is often regarded now as one of the minor cornerstones of our foreign policy. Some people think that the commonwealth is now little more than something we make gestures toward in afterdinner speeches. But are we satisfied with merely cherishing our membership in this body which we did so much to found, in which we did so much to adjust and develop toward changing conditions? I am wondering whether we can find a unique and more worth-while role within the commonwealth.
The question of external aid is an important one. With many people this is a popular field of endeavour. But are we at our most effective here? Can we improve our contribution toward a peaceful and better world? Should we specialize in aid, which perforce cannot be unlimited? Should we establish priorities and, if so, what are they to be? Should we assist the commonwealth, Latin America, the Caribbean or French speaking Africa? Should we emphasize bilateral aid or


channel all our aid through multilateral, universal programs? I have heard all these suggestions made, as I am sure have other hon. members.
Should we not also look, Mr. Speaker, at our own diplomatic arm? Should we not ask ourselves whether we are satisfied with our foreign service? There are many areas in the globe where Canada has no representation. We talk about a two-China policy; yet we do not have ambassadors in either China. There are many parts of Asia in which we have no diplomatic representation. Asia is a continent where millions and millions of people live and on the future of which depends so much the fate of all mankind. Asia is the most expanding and expansive part of the world.
These questions cannot be simply answered, Mr. Speaker; they can merely be raised, as I do raise them, considering that these aspects are extremely important to the economic facts of our domestic life.
When I last spoke on this subject I urged the Secretary of State for External Affairs to be more forthcoming in his discussions of this important realm. I was not suggesting that he come into the house and tell us, for instance, what the ambassador from Indonesia had told him. This, of course, was not what was in my mind. But I do believe that foreign policy, which as the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) discovered in his poll is of absorbing interest to our people, should command more attention in this house.
I hope that the standing committee on external affairs will continue the program it began earlier in the session whereby for the first time the committee looked at areas of interest and studied in depth some of our problems, bringing before it experts other than those in the department. I think this is extremely valuable and important.
It is so easy in this day of the mass media to grasp at seemingly simple solutions. In our yearning for peace there is the danger of being satisfied with those courses of action that are suggested by some of the more vocal but not necessarily the more thoughtful elements of the public. For instance, to call upon the United States unilaterally to stop bombing North Viet Nam seems a proper course. It seems to put us on the side of the angels which is where we all want to be. But to offer advice to the United States might not be so effective as may appear, or as we wish it to appear. Of course we want the bombing stopped. Of course any thoughtful Canadian is filled with anxiety and worse at the increasing engagement in this conflict of United
October 10, 1987

States personnel. Should a thoughtful person not seek evidence that any such cessation now would be more efficacious than the several which have already taken place? Is that not the thoughtful course of action?
For a long time many proclaimed that recognition of Peking and the admission of that regime to the UN was the greatest step to world peace. This recipe has been less frequently advanced in recent months. Not long ago the call was to have South Africa kicked out of the Commonwealth and all would be well. Something like that did happen, but nothing happened to the victims of the repressive racist government of that country.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I suggest that we ought to devote more time to this subject, that we should seek to reappraise, to bring a greater depth to our discussion. Foreign policy is no longer an esoteric field, the preserve of a few specialists. We who represent the people who will suffer the results of the failure of world diplomacy dare not miss opportunities to enlighten ourselves and the people we represent in foreign affairs. If we fail, that which we plan domestically through budgets, legislation or other parliamentary means will be of no avail.
If there is one hopeful aspect in the less than glorious performance of the present government it is that through its weakness and indecision as an executive it has enhanced the scope and stature of the legislative branch. Perhaps in the revival of committees and the establishment of new areas of activity for them we shall produce a much healthier political society in this country and bring about a more valuable parliamentary institution. For that we should be indeed grateful. I suggest that one area where such a revitalized branch of our system would be of tremendous importance is the terribly difficult field of foreign policy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume it is proper for me to say that this is my thanksgiving budget speech. Regardless of the government in power or our social and economic problems, I think we should all be thankful to live in Canada and for the opportunities that we have at this time to enjoy life in this country. Before proceeding farther I must say to the minister that I offer him my sympathy, my sarcasm and my suggestions in a spirit of good will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext:
I am grateful.
The Budget-Mr. Herridge

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Our over-all problems which have been recognized by members of this house and the Canadian people in general have been stated before. They are the preservation of world peace and the maintenance of national unity. I might say in that respect that I have no hesitation in saying that any party or member of this house approaching the question of national unity with a view to party advantage is doing this country a great disfavour.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While we may have different points of view we must present them properly and must approach this problem in the spirit that it is a national emergency.
We all recognize that inflation and its effect on the cost of living and the cost of housing is a serious problem at this time. I am not one, Mr. Speaker, who rises in a glib way to say that I have answers to all our problems at this time, but I shall have a few suggestions to make later.
In my opinion this debate has been worth while. The minister has had the opportunity to hear the opinions of the Canadian people expressed by members of the opposition parties and in some instances by members on the government side of the house. I am sure that we have listened with interest to the minister's statements which, in the language of the Financial Times, were a mixture of sermonizing and action. I have enjoyed both aspects. I am sure we all agree with the minister that there is a need for fiscal and monetary stability. Anyone with a sense of responsibility accepts that. There is a need for priorities in programs and expenditures. That is easy to suggest but no doubt in some instances those priorities must be arrived at as a result of consultation with the provinces and agreements on that basis.
There is an urgent need to provide capital for housing, particularly for those who are unable to obtain their own housing or pay the costs involved at the present time. There is a great need for serviced land in the larger centres. Without doubt there is a need for planned urban development.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not like the general attitude that we should accept as inevitable the continued drift to the metropolitan areas and cities. I have lived in a different atmosphere. I read Ruskin, Morris, and others like them representative of the later Victorian period. I did not look forward

October 10, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Herridge to a society composed of centralized populations. I did not have any politics in my youth. Later I was a Liberal, but I think I have advanced a bit since those days.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I looked forward to a society where man would enjoy greater happiness through the decentralization of populations to towns, small communities and rural centres, and the decentralization of industry. I know that people move to where the jobs are, but I think we must give some thought to the decentralization of population and industry in this country.
I was interested in the minister's proposal to ease the tax burden on low income groups that require housing. We all look forward to a further explanation of that proposal. If the government continues to insist on maintaining the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials I trust that some method will be devised to assist the low income group. We all agree with the necessity for restraint in government expenditures and with respect to prices and costs. That will be a matter for considerable discussion in the near future. Though we agree with restraint and though I trust we shall seek to economize where possible, we must not overlook the needs of the veterans and their dependents with respect to increases in disability pensions and war veterans allowances in the near future. These are the men who defended our country, who upheld our freedom in at least two world wars.
I have received letters from my constituents complaining of two things in particular. The first is the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. I have a letter from a gentleman who is an official of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada. It is a thoughtful letter and deals with the question seriously on the basis of his observations of the effect of this tax on house building as it comes within his knowledge. He suggests that the government would be wise to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
The other criticism I have had is largely from corporate organizations-municipalities and similar bodies-with respect to the increase in the interest rate on housing mortgages. I wish to read a letter from the deputy city clerk of the corporation of the city of Trail.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Dear Sir:
The council of the city of Trail are greatly concerned over the recently announced increase in

the interest rate of 8\ per cent for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation financing of housing loans.
The council would like to see a reconsideration of this increase as they feel some measure has to be taken to stimulate housing construction in areas such as our Glenmerry subdivision.
Thank you for your kind attention to this matter.
Yours very truly,

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK

speechtext:
I read this one letter from the numerous letters I have received to the same effect from municipalities and organizations because I believe there is a great deal of validity in the objection made. Earlier speakers from this group have dealt in detail and at great length with this subject. They have expressed both general and local criticism of the budget's shortcomings and of our monetary and fiscal policies. I shall not repeat what they have said in their contributions to this debate.
I was particularly interested in the speech made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It contained numerous suggestions as to ways in which the government could reduce its expenditures. I followed carefully the speech made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) with its caustic criticism of unnecessary government spending and I listened with interest a few minutes ago to what I thought was a very constructive speech by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie). I also listened with particular attention to the speech of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon), and I quote from Hansard of October 5, page 2865, to emphasize briefly what he had to say and to make certain that many people Who will read the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay West and who may not read the speech made by the President of the Privy Council will know what views he expressed. Referring to something which had been said earlier by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) commented:
On that occasion I think he said the things that are in the hearts and minds of all of us. We all know that no defence is really effective any more in this world except peace. If we kid ourselves that anything else will be effective, we are very foolish indeed.
We have a second problem that is perhaps closer to us here and we are very much aware of it. That is the question of the continuation of confederation and the unity of our country.
I turn now to page 2866. The President of the Privy Council was interrupted by someone. It would not have been by me; some
October 10, 1967	COMMONS
Conservative must have interjected. He went on to say:
Let us not be silly.
Not only have we the problem of obtaining peace in the world in which we live, not only have we the problem of achieving unity within our country, but we also have the problem, living next door to the greatest nation in the world, of maintaining our own independence. Most of us in one way or another are searching for the solution to that problem. I hope that before very many months have passed, the government will be able to table a white paper which will at least provide a focus for debate about what should be done in this respect.
I heartily sympathize with the concern shown by the President of the Privy Council in regard to the search for peace, Canadian unity and Canadian economic independence and I am one of those who look forward to reading the white paper on economic independence when it is issued.
In this connection and before proceeding further I should like to put on record the contents of a note compiled as a result of research done by a friend of mine and having to do with Canadian economic independence. My sentiments on this subject are entirely in accord with those of the President of the Privy Council. Anyway, these are my friend's findings. Based on information culled from Dominion Bureau of Statistics publications he has found it possible to make a good estimate of the extent of post-war United States direct investment in Canada. The figures show that over the 1946-1964 period a total figure of $10.6 billion was made up of $5.2 billion of undistributed profits held in Canada and various accounting adjustments and revaluations. From a sample of eight out of the 19 years, however, it appears that dividends remitted from the United States controlled corporations in Canada must have totalled about $5.4 billion.
