speechtext:
I will supply that later.
So more than the equivalent of what gets into the statistics as net capital inflow was covered by dividends going out of Canada to the United States owners. In other words, more than the total increase in United States direct investment in Canada since the war was covered by profits made in Canada. I think he makes a very good point. The gentleman in question is-as a matter of fact, I do not have his name on the document and I have forgotten it at the moment but I will see that the hon. gentleman gets it later.
DEBATES	2943
The Budget-Mr. Herridge
Now I wish to make a few other suggestions. Suggestions have already been made concerning means by which the expenditures of the various departments might be reduced, how we could lessen our budget deficit and so on. I again urge the government to use the Bank of Canada to provide the social capital required by provincial and municipal governments for investment in housing, hospitals, schools, highways and other public projects. Last night I read in the Ottawa Citizen a story headlined: "City Finds U.S. Loan Is Cheaper". It began:
City hall will try to counter the soaring Canadian interest rate by borrowing $16,183,000 in the United States.
Financial authorities have assured the city funds will be available in the U.S. at an effective interest rate of 6.47 per cent.
I simply cannot understand why the city of Ottawa should have to go to the United States to borrow money with a consequent outflow of interest on this loan and many others like it. From the statistics I have been able to gather in the last few weeks, we have borrowed in the neighbourhood of $1 billion from the United States already this year. I cannot understand why the Bank of Canada cannot provide loans to cover expenditures of this sort at a rate of interest which would meet administrative and other costs without any loss to the government of Canada. When the minister replies later I wish he would inform me why this cannot be done. I understand it is done now to some extent in certain circumstances. I would like the minister to tell us why it cannot be done on all such occasions. There seems to be some hidden reason for not doing so. I have been told there are psychological reasons for not going further in this direction.
We in our party have urged this method of financing for many years. Only a few months ago my leader, in a letter on this subject, endorsed the idea wholeheartedly, so I have no hesitation in bringing up the matter at this time. I might add that we could continue to use the Industrial Development Bank to meet the needs of small and medium-sized industries and leave the rest of the banking business to the private banking concerns under present circumstances when a new competitive spirit seems to be rising.
I wish to deal now with another matter. We have learned how we can save a few thousand dollars here and a few million there. Again I wish to tell the house that we could save a great deal more money if we were to withdraw from NATO. If we are to
2944	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Herridge meet our responsibilities to the underdeveloped nations as well as our own responsibilities here in Canada, we simply cannot continue to carry on our present expenditures in the military field. We have to make a choice. In that connection I wish to quote a statement made by our leader, as reported in the Globe and Mail of Sept. 14, 1967. The report is headed, "Pull Canada Out of NATO, Douglas Says." It reads:
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Canada should withdraw its military support of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and press for a complete overhaul of the defence pact, says T. C. Douglas, national leader of the New Democratic Party.
Mr. Douglas told 300 Simon Fraser University students that perpetuation of NATO is another example of Canada's slavishly following an obsolete U.S. foreign policy.
"I believe as far as Canada is concerned, we're wasting our money in NATO," he said. ''The world has changed, but U.S. and Canadian foreign policy has not changed with world conditions."
Mr. Douglas said NATO should be used to negotiate peace, not war. He said the organization is based on policies that assume the Soviet Union is a monolith dedicated to subverting the entire world.
"We cannot resolve the problems of a revolutionary age by winning military victories," the N.D.P. leader said. "We are not going to stop change with arms. If Canada is going to contribute to the peace ol the world, we must lay down a policy not overshadowed by the United States or any other country."
I think our leader is on very sound grounds on this question.
At the present time we are spending $1,688 million on national defence, which according to my calculations is between 20 per cent and 25 per cent of our national budget. To illustrate this, Canada's contribution to the infrastructure of the NATO program was $152,-
300,000	at March 31, 1966. The estimated cost of the aircraft supplied to NATO to April 30, 1966, amounts to $211,600,000. The capital cost of fixed facilities at the base is estimated to be $14,700,000. The total estimated annual cost of maintaining No. 1 air division in NATO is $85,300,000. The estimated annual cost of maintaining our brigade group in NATO is $64,500,000. The estimated annual cost of transporting defence forces and their dependents is $7,500,000, making a total cost of $535,900,000. Again I say I do not see how we can continue these expenditures and meet our responsibilities at home and abroad.
I turn now to NORAD, and in that connection I wish to quote from an interesting article by John Gellner which appeared in the

DEBATES	October 10, 1967
Globe and Mail on October 9, 1967. Its heading is, "A Price Canada Will Have To Pay To Stay in NORAD," and I quote two paragraphs:
With the YF-12, or whatever it will ultimately be called (Y denotes an experimental type), will go an improved air-to-air missile, AIM-47, and a new airborne warning and control system. The latter, carried in huge jet transports or converted bombers, will apparently replace all that NORAD has in the way of electronic ground environment, although the DEW line might retain some limited uses.
One can only speculate what such rearmament might cost Canada. An educated guess based on the assumption that Canada's present three CF-101 and two Bomarc squadrons would be replaced by two squadrons of YF-12's-say 30 aircraft, with the essential spares and handling equipment-should cost something like $500 million. Adding the price of installations and training, and of Canada's participation, with aircraft and equipment, the total bill would probably not be much less than $1 billion.
Mr. Gellner is a writer on military subjects and apparently has made a close study of this matter. I hope that these costs to the Canadian people will be considered when the government deals with the negotiations in connection with the NORAD agreement.
Again I want to say that for years it has been our policy to oppose nuclear weapons on Canadian soil and in the hands of Canadian troops anywhere. Last year the then minister of national defence informed the house that, "The R.C.A.F. now has available to it in Europe an explosive power comparable to several thousand times that used at Hiroshima." What a reversal of the minister's stand when he was in opposition. Then he was firmly opposed to nuclear weapons, and I well remember sitting in the house and listening to the speech he made on that occasion. I hope the government will reverse this policy and use the money which we are spending on defence for other purposes.
As a matter of fact, two or three years ago the German ambassador, in a speech at Winnipeg, said something to the effect that while Canada's contribution to NATO is not of great military effect its position in NATO has a certain morale building value. Surely we can use this money to better advantage for ourselves and in assisting the underdeveloped nations.
While I know we have the support of the President of the Privy Council on this issue, I wish to quote two paragraphs from the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in his Nobel peace prize lecture delivered at Oslo, Norway, on December 11, 1957, titled "The Four Faces Of Peace":
Today, less than ever, can we defend ourselves by force for there is no effective defence against
October 10, 1967

the all-destroying effect of nuclear missile weapons. Indeed their very power has made their use Intolerable, even unthinkable, because of the anni-hilative retaliation in kind that such use would invoke. So peace remains, as the phrase goes, balanced uneasily on terror and the use of maximum force is frustrated by the certainty that it will be used in reply with a totally devastating effect. Peace, however, must surely be more than this trembling rejection of universal suicide.
The stark and inescapable fact is that today we cannot defend our society by war since total war is total destruction, and if war is used as an instrument of policy, eventually we will have total war. Therefore, the best defence of peace is not power, but the removal of the causes of war, and international agreements which will put peace on a stronger foundation than the terror of destruction.
I must say we can all agree with those words, and I quote the Prime Minister to show we have got him on our side so far as principle and spirit are concerned.
While we all realize we must solve our immediate problems with respect to fiscal and monetary stability and the need for priorities, we must also relate these matters to the need for a resources development and investment program in co-operation with the provinces. Unless we can conserve and develop our natural resources on sound principles we will not be able to maintain or improve our standard of living in the future.
In my opinion, if we are going to meet our obligations to the underdeveloped nations food is the first essential. If we have food we can afford to say "man shall not live by bread alone," but if we do not have food there is nothing to say. So accustomed are we in Canada to the well stocked larder and the overladen plate that it is almost impossible for some of us to imagine what life is like for those hanging over the brink of starvation in other countries.
The first requirements of human beings in the underdeveloped countries are food, clothing and shelter, and assistance in building their economies so that they can produce more of their own requirements as the years go by. We have the resources to accept our moral responsibility if we are willing to prime our expenditures on defence accordingly. In my opinion we cannot afford to go on spending these large amounts on defence and at the same time try to meet our responsibilities to our people at home and to people abroad.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Our natural resources are, first, water, land, forests and minerals, and very briefly I wish to indicate how improvident we have been in dealing with Canadian water supplies 27053-187
The Budget-Mr. Herridge to date. Later I shall deal with this matter at great length. I should like to quote briefly from an article in the September issue of Electric Light and Power, a magazine published in Boston, in which they begin to let the cat out of the bag about the Columbia River treaty. As you know the power production there has been increased to 9.2 million kilowatts although we only get paid for 1.2 million in the treaty. The article reads as follows:
Favourable Payout.

Thus, according to the Dept, of Interior, the total average annual benefits of $45,697,000 would exceed annual costs by $31,000,000 for a benefit-to-cost ratio of 3.1:1. In addition the article states:
Nearly 500,000 acres, approximately half of the ultimate 1,029,000 acres to be developed on the Columbia Basin project, now have irrigation service available. The annual gross value of crops produced on the project's irrigated lands now exceeds $71 million.
We are shipping our water across to the United States and they are using it to irrigate
500,000	acres at the present time. They intend to irrigate over one million acres and are sending their products back into Canada where they compete very easily with the products of Canadian producers because of the circumstances under which they produce at the present time.
I am having some tables worked out in this regard by a very competent engineer and I will deal with this matter more fully later. I should like to suggest, however, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) and his officials should take the first opportunity to read this article which indicates what is happening in the United States at the present time with regard to the further development of the Columbia River.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Mackasey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey faced with the need for more participation by real French speaking Canadians at the top level in our large corporations. We will still need a capital that is more representative of the two founding races and a capital district which will make sure that Hull will finally reap some of the economic benefits of a capital district. We will still be faced with the problem of providing Quebec with all the assistance needed to facilitate communication with other countries which share its language. These are but some of the problems which must be resolved whether or not during the week end in Quebec it is decided that it is economically or uneconomically sound to separate.
I agree with the determination of the Minister of Finance to reduce spending next year and cut back on expenditures wherever possible in order to fight inflation, but I must also point out that the real danger from separatism in the future in Quebec lies not in the arguments of the academics or intellectuals but in the poverty of too many people in too many areas of Quebec. Too many people in Quebec, in spite of the fact we are experiencing the biggest and longest boom in our history, still live in squalor. Too many people have been bypassed for geographical reasons in this affluent society. Too many people live on incomes well under the $4,000 per annum mark. These people could very well be the separatists of the future, and when the separatist movement spreads to these areas, when the false doctrine of separatism finally catches on in these regions, then the possibility of the end of this country will be more real than it is today.
Perhaps there are some of you who think I am exaggerating, but I can look back at speeches I made in this house five years ago at which time I made the same predictions and the same analysis when Social Credit spread across the province of Quebec. What I said then was certainly not intended to hurt the feelings of my friends in the Ralliement des Creditistes, who by their prodding have done much to improve the working conditions in this house for those of the French language. The people endorsed the Social Credit movement then because they felt they had nothing to lose. They endorsed it in a spirit of despair and defeatism.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The best weapon we have against separatism is the elimination of poverty in those regions which for too long have been limited to a mere subsistence level, with the people


forced to till uneconomic farms, forced to accept welfare payments for survival. Poverty that strips the father of a family of his dignity breeds resentment, discontent, unrest and will eventually, I am sorry to predict, breed separatism. Our friends in the R.I.N. know this. Our separatist friend in the far corner of the house knows this. It is in that area of the province that the R.I.N. will devote its time in the future. Ironically, if we were to canvass that area today we would probably find greater support for federalism than anywhere else. Why? It is because, having so little, they fear any movement that might take that little away from them, even temporarily. But there does come a time in the history of all nations and of all peoples when they say, "Well, if I am going to starve I might as well starve under a new system." They could very easily say, "If I am going to starve it might as well be in the new country of Quebec as in the present country of Canada."
Historians in the house know better than I that this is true. The Irish rebellion, and particularly the unrest before it, caused economic hardships in that wonderful country from which they have still not recovered. But you and I know that if we discuss that rebellion with the people of Ireland today, despite their economic problems they will tell us it was worth while.
The other evening a very close friend of mine who has been kind to me since I entered politics suggested that perhaps the English speaking minority in Quebec ranks with the most unpopular of minorities anywhere in the world today. At first I was upset at the thought but upon reflection I had to agree that perhaps there is much truth in this suggestion, and I wondered precisely why. I came to the conclusion that it is perhaps because of the absence of a dialogue, the type of dialogue to which Claude Ryan refers, between the English speaking and the French speaking people of Quebec. In too many instances that lack of dialogue has left French speaking Canadians with a stereotyped concept of what an English speaking Quebecker has been responsible for in the past in that province. We must remember that while the non-French population of Quebec numbers
1,200,000	people, more people, for instance, than make up the population of Saskatchewan, most of that population is situated in the greater Montreal area, so that one out of every three can be classified as non-French speaking. Therefore, contrary to public opinion, in many parts of Quebec there is little or
October 10, 1967

no contact culturally between English speaking Canadians and French speaking Canadians, and direct confrontation or communication therefore is limited all too frequently to business hours.
To the people particularly who have little or no contact with the English speaking minority, we represent in Quebec the absentee owner who for years exploited the labour class by denying them the right to join a union and paid them low salaries and wages under the pretence that this had to be done in order to compete with other provinces or other areas of greater productivity. We represent to many in the remote regions the large, foreign-owned corporations that ravaged our forests or shipped tons and tons of primary ores from Quebec to be returned later in the form of finished products. We represent the almost non-existent but still very legendary figure residing in Westmount, manipulating the strings that activate St. James Street.
Nobody bothers to point out that these things happened in a day long past and that the city of Westmount is today composed almost equally of French speaking and English speaking Canadians. Nobody from French Canada takes the trouble to point out that the ravaging of our forests and the excessive control over Quebec's primary products was possible only with the full co-operation of French speaking politicians, Liberal and otherwise, who were returned in election after election by the French speaking majority of Quebec.
The dialogue which is so necessary in the opinion of Claude Ryan, and I share that opinion, would be much easier if French speaking Canada were to recognize that the English speaking minority that lives in my city of Verdun, for instance, is much more representative of English Quebec not only today but in reality for some considerable time. When I discuss, as I often do, in mixed company the complaints that French speaking Canadians have about confederation, the English speaking Quebeckers of Verdun quite often ask, "What am I guilty of" or, "How did I contribute to the present tension in this province, in this city or in this country?" They point out that their only contact with French speaking Canadians comes at work with the Northern Electric Company, Bell Telephone, Canadair or the railways. They say, "We have the same rate of pay. We do the same job. We reap the same benefits and suffer the same hardships as the worker from French Canada." They are puzzled, to a certain degree with justification.
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
Others say, "I married a French speaking girl. I get along wonderfully well with her relatives and she with mine," etc. Others say, "Our children play on the same hockey team. What am I guilty of? What is the English, speaking minority of a working class district-such as mine really guilty of other than not communicating enough?" But that is the fault of all Quebeckers, French speaking and' English speaking; we all share the blame for this.
Much of the friction in that province could be eliminated if in French speaking Canada the people would understand that those who admittedly kept Quebec poor when they could have contributed more positively to its growth are not representative of the minority in the province, and that those who exploited Quebec in the past could do so only with the co-operation of French speaking leaders both in and out of politics. Our dialogue would also be more fruitful if perhaps some of the misconceptions about French Canada and French speaking Quebeckers were erased. Expo and the student exchange program this year have done a great deal to portray my province more accurately. Not all French speaking Canadians are called Jean-Baptiste. Not every family contains a priest, a nun or a brother amongst its children. Not all university graduates are lawyers or notaries. While the English speaking universities-I am sure the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquar-rie) is more familiar with this subject than I-in this country are rediscovering the humanities, the French institutions of learning are turning out engineers, scientists, physicists and graduates from the new faculties of commerce. They are entering and competing successfully in those fields of finance dominated previously by English speaking Canadians.
Today more graduates of French universities are joining the ranks of the federal civil service than ever before. At least, this has been the situation in the last three or four years for which I have looked up the statistics. Today more than ever before representatives of French speaking Canada are working quietly and effectively side by side with their English speaking friends preparing for the future of this country.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I hope that the economic realities of the day, the cut-backs contemplated by the Minister of Finance, in no way restrict the economic growth of Quebec or in any way affect the development of those regions

October 10, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Pascoe which, as 1 stated earlier, are the potential source of separatism in the future. Quebec cannot stand any further increase in the rate of unemployment.
Quebec needs more secondary industry than ever before in its history. The labour strife that has marred the Quebec scene lately must be viewed in its total perspective. We must realize that for every strike there are hundreds of wage agreements reached and concluded with a minimum of fanfare in the province. Quebec has an ever-increasing source of skilled labour. The average worker in my province is conscientious and, given the proper opportunity, he will prove to be as productive as the worker in any other province.
Businessmen anxious to protect their present investments, Canadians anxious for this country to reach its potential, people everywhere anxious to remain united, should realize that this is not the time to find consolation in economic arguments against the validity or feasibility of separatism. This is not the time for blackmail or threats; it is not the time to take fixed positions. It is the time for dialogue, for communication, for sacrifice, for understanding.
I am more than ever convinced that in the proper relationship between the two founding races of this country lies our best defence against assimilation by the United States of America. I am convinced that it is under the form of federalism that the best safeguards exist for the continuation of the French language and French culture. These solutions should prove to be little problem, Mr. Speaker, now that sane voices are finally speaking out. As Claude Ryan so aptly put it recently in a thought-provoking editorial, federalism over the last 100 years has made possible in this country freedom of opinion, freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly. What other system, Mr. Speaker, could have done as much?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the budget debate goes into its fourth day it should be made clear that we are following established procedure. Under the rules of parliament six days are allocated to the budget debate. As is the practice in everv parliament in Canada, the opposition voices strong criticism of government policies and moves amendments which, of course, the government regards as votes of non-confidence
From headlines such as those in the Ottawa Journal for Friday, October 6, which stated

"Grits Survive Another Non-confidence Vote", the public might receive the impression that we are taking up time in unnecessary talk. I just want to make it clear that this is a six-day debate according to the rules of parliament.
In this same vein of informing the public about what we in parliament are doing I should like to press my arguments a little further. Shortly before the resumption of parliament the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) outlined a list of 25 important pieces of legislation and 15 other items which he requested parliament to pass before the Christmas recess. I believe that press gallery writers and commentators worked this out to mean that 40 pieces of legislation had to be considered and approved in 45 actual sitting days. The Liberal press as usual has followed the government line. Articles have been written and comments made about the duty of opposition members to oblige the government by passing legislation, as if through the means of some sort of mass production mechanism. According to these Liberal propagandists we must curtail our criticism, limit our debate and give our blessing to all government programs.
Our system of parliamentary democracy does not work in this way, Mr. Speaker. Those who are attempting to pressure the opposition into passing so much legislation in so few days are conveniently trying to forget opposition attitudes from 1955 to 1963. In those days many of those who now sit on the government side sat in opposition, and it is a matter of record how they criticized and delayed measures.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the house to two or three opinions expressed by opposition members of the day who now sit on the government side. The Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), who in 1962 sat on this side of the house, was very vocal in her criticism. As reported on page 227 of Hansard for October 4, 1962, she said:
All members of the opposition were elected for one purpose, and that was in opposition to the government.
As reported on page 398 of Hansard for October 11 of the same year, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) said:
Since it is the duty of members of the loyal opposition to oppose, I cannot see how one can bn'-? effective opposition without constructive criticism.
October 10, 1967

Lastly, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, speaking in the house on February 4, 1963, said as reported on page 3409 of Hansard:
So, Mr. Speaker, surely it is the duty of all members of the opposition in this house to give the people a chance to return what they would consider to be a better government. We can only do that by getting rid of this one, and that can only be done by taking a united stand.
I have quoted those extracts, Mr. Speaker, to show the change in attitude on the government side today. These quotations represented the v.ews of some hon. gentlemen opposite when they were sitting on the opposition side, and they certainly lived up to those views at that time. They now want to limit criticism by hon. members of the opposition by introducing new rules, some of which I favour, though not to the extent of limiting debate.
The debate so far has been very interesting and I congratulate those who have spoken. The arguments have been very direct and opposition members have emphasized a genuine concern about the present economic situation in Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) very casually described the situation as a heated economy. We agree that there is a heated economy in Canada, and we are trying to put heat on the government to take effective action to combat inflation and control prices of consumer goods and services. In regard to the heated economy perhaps I may be allowed to paraphrase a historical quotation and say that this government fiddles while the heated economy burns.
The Minister of Finance said, as reported on page 2808 of Hansard for October 4:
The undesirable rate of increases in prices and costs to which I referred on June 1 has continued.
Then, as reported at page 2809 he admitted that:
*-the rate of increase in costs and prices is still much too high.
We in the opposition certainly agree with that, Mr. Speaker.
In the Canadian Statistical Review issued in September by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics there are charts which definitely show the steady rise in consumer prices and the steady rise in the cost of food. I commend these charts to the Minister of Finance.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In this regard I have also received a copy of a letter from the president of an association called "Women Against Soaring Prices," the original of which was sent to the Prime Minister. The writer talks of a petition and asks for an appointment at early convenience
The Budget-Mr. Pascoe to discuss "with you what can be done to combat soaring prices on essential foods and skyrocketing rentals."
I also received a letter from a constituent who of necessity must buy drugs. She sent me bills for drugs which she had purchased on April 6, 1967 and April 25, 1967. The serial number of the prescription is given. On April 6 the drug cost $1.70; on April 25 the same drug with the same serial number cost $2.90, an increase of $1.20, as noted on the second bill. The April 25 bill has this notation also: "N.B. There has been a price increase on this prescription in compliance with the new pricing schedule. Thank you."
May I draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to the report of the thirtieth annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. Glancing through this publication I find this statement:
More than half of the 35 resolutions adopted sought increased federal financial assistance, directly or indirectly, for municipalities.
The list of these resolutions has been published. I quoted that paragraph to show the need for the government to take definite action with respect to our present economic situation. As I have said, other members of the opposition have dealt fully with housing costs, high interest rates and the ever-increasing costs of consumer goods and services. Those hon. members offered the Minister of Finance excellent advice.
I now wish to speak about another problem that ought to worry the government but does not seem to. I have a suggestion to make which could help our economy and bring in extra revenue for the government. The Minister of Finance, as well as the Minister of National Revenue, will be pleased that my suggestion will not entail a drain on the federal treasury. It would, in fact, add to the government's cash intake. All that is required is more direct action. Actually, greater sales effort is required.
I refer to the recent drop in wheat prices and the export sales of wheat. Some on the other side of the house may say that this is purely a western problem, but this would be a narrow attitude to take. Wheat prices and sales are of vital concern to the whole Canadian economy. This is acknowledged. For the sceptics on the government side may I refer to the 1963 report of the Bank of Canada and to a statement on wheat by its governor, Mr. Louis Rasminsky. In his report Mr. Rasminsky revealed that export wheat sales saved Canada from a foreign exchange

October 10, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Pascoe crisis. He said that a threatened run on the Canadian dollar was prevented by large sales of Canadian wheat and flour. Incidentally, these large wheat sales were to the Soviet union under contracts made possible by the initiative of the Diefenbaker government. Mr. Rasminsky reviewed the situation and the value of Canadian wheat exports and said that these exceptionally large export sales dispelled immediate concern about the possibility of renewed foreign exchange difficulties.
The wheat problem can best be summarized by reading briefly from a brief article published in the Monetary Times for October, 1967, captioned "Saskatchewan Wheat Pool." It is headed "A Serious Situation" and reads in part as follows:
The 1967 crop is almost all In the bin but the prospects are bleak for its sale at a reasonable price.
The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is very concerned about this situation and is working hard to try to remedy it.
This article was written before the wheat had been completely harvested. It is all in bins now. It continues:
Chas. W. Gibbings, Pool president, has said that Canadian wheat producers are facing the most critical marketing situation that has existed for more than 20 years. The price of Canadian wheat (at September 8) -
We have seen recent developments. This refers to September 8.
-has fallen by 22 cents a bushel. The price has been forced down to meet the competition presented by policies of other exporters.
The international wheat agreement lapsed on July 31 and a new one negotiated under GATT at Geneva cannot become effective until next July 1.
I now wish to refer to the "Wheat Review". Before doing so, may I say that I have talked to leaders of farm organizations who are concerned with this matter. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics publication dramatically illustrates the drop in wheat exports.

Mr. Ralph Cov/an (York-Humber):	Mr. Speaker, before making some direct comments on the budget and estimates for 19671968, I want to take advantage of the traditional leeway that is always extended during the budget debate to refer to some remarks I made in the house last Monday evening regarding payments to hospitals in Quebec. This also, of course, is covered by our own federal estimates under the Hospital Services and Diagnostic Treatment Act.
Some hon. members, particularly those of you from the province of Quebec, may have noted the tremendous furore on the radio and television, and in newspapers in Quebec, with regard to my statement that the hospitals in Quebec were six months behind in the receipt of moneys from the provincial department of health in Quebec. I have no reason whatever to change one iota, one syllable or one word of what I said a week ago last night in this house. I would simply like to add a few remarks to those I made then.
A very highly placed official in the Quebec government called me long distance from Quebec city on Tuesday. He wished to discuss my remarks with me, and I was glad to talk with him. He emphasized, without any heat, that twice a month the Quebec department of health sends cheques to the hospitals in Quebec, on the 10th and 25th of the month. I said to him, "I have never denied you send cheques to the hospitals on the 10th and 25th of each month, if these are your remittance dates, but what I would like to point out to you is that the cheques you sent out in September covered expenses incurred by the

hospitals as far back as February and March, which simply means that the hospitals in Quebec, or the boards of trustees, have themselves had to raise the money for the intervening six months to pay their staffs."
Since then, I have had several hospitals in Quebec telephone me. One hospital in particular wished to know if it was included in the four to which I made indirect reference, and I replied no, that I had not been speaking to any official of that hospital. The spokesman then said, "Count us in, that will make five."
This hospital, I believe the largest in the province of Quebec, to my surprise pointed out to me that when the individual hospitals submit their annual budgets to the Quebec department of health at the end of a calendar year, forecasting their expenditures for the coming 12 months, they do not hear from the Quebec government until possibly July or August. These hospitals have gone along in January, February, March, April, May, or what have you, spending according to the regular details of their submitted budgets. Then, in the summer, they may get word from the Quebec department saying, "We are cutting you back 20 per cent." In effect, the department does not approve a budget submitted at least seven months previously until the government's own good time.
I exceedingly regret the situation in the province of Quebec in this regard. I do believe that the federal government should have the right to demand an accounting of the expenditure of the funds it sends to the province of Quebec to be spent on hospital care under the Hospital Services and Diagnostic Treatment Act. True enough, this money comes under the Interim Financial Arrangements Act.
Last Tuesday, when I pointed out to the very highly placed official in Quebec that although the hospitals there are getting their cheques on the 10th and 25th of the month, but in September they were getting paid for March expenses, he completely changed the subject and said to me, "We in Quebec city have never received a cheque from the federal government for 13 months for hospital services."
You know, Mr. Speaker, the statement the gentleman made was correct. They have not received a cheque from the federal government for 13 months for hospital purposes because under the agreement between the province of Quebec and the federal government the money reaches Quebec under the
October 10, 1967

Interim Financial Arrangements Act, and of course the cheques do not have on them, "For hospital purposes." But the federal government is sitting here passing this legislation, passing these accounts in order that this money may be available for hospital purposes.
I immediately re-checked with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) and with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) because on Monday morning, a week ago, they had assured me everything that was due to Quebec was up to date. They reassured me on Tuesday afternoon, although they did not need to because I have every confidence that anything paid through the federal government to Quebec under the Interim Financial Arrangements Act is up to date. I just make these comments in passing because I regret the situation, and I wish it could be cleared up to the satisfaction of the hospitals and of their boards of trustees in the province of Quebec.
I am now anxious to make a few comments with regard to a budgetary item in the blue book-

I wish to refer to the budgetary item under the Treasury Board to be found at page 560 of the blue book-Contingencies, subject to the approval of the Treasury Board, $45 million. This is the contingency item of the Treasury Board about which there was considerable discussion and debate in November of last year. I spoke in November of last year and stated at that time that I regretted exceedingly the action of this
The Budget-Mr. Cowan administration in having paid the civil service in mid-November in the manner in which they did. I said it was a denial of democracy. I repeat tonight that the method of paying the civil service in mid-November last year was a denial of democracy and that a subterfuge was used in order to get around an interim supply vote. As a Liberal, born and bred, I regret exceedingly that the party to which I belong should indulge in such practices. I regret that this is the first opportunity I have had to speak on the matter in any detail, but I am taking the first opportunity to do so.
I should like to state that I consider the present actions of the cabinet a mockery of democracy and I am heartsick over the matter. This of course brings up the question, who is or what is the government at the present time? You will find in the parliamentary library a fine book by R. MacGregor Dawson who wrote a biography of Mackenzie King with which most of us are familiar. In 1949 he issued a book entitled "Democratic Government in Canada". On page 1 of this book we read this:
The first and most important characteristic of Canadian government is that it is a democracy, a government which is controlled by the greater part of the people. It rests on the will of the people and is at all times responsive to their opinions.
Then on page 5 we find the following:
Representative government (means) "Representatives" are elected to speak and act for groups of voters in association with representatives who have been similarly chosen by voters in other areas in the nation. The Canadian House of Commons (is) composed of such representatives elected by the people to act in their name and on their behalf.
It is true enough that we have representatives elected to the Canadian House of Commons ostensibly to act on our behalf, but I say to you that the representatives here are never consulted by the administration. We are members of parliament representing in some cases as many as 350,000 people. The first we ever see of a cabinet bill is when it is laid on our desks and we are not supposed to vote against it because this would make us rebels or heretics. I have no idea what the cabinet's estimation is of the intelligence of a private member when they expect to be able to place a bill before a private member which he has never seen and expect him not to question the contents of it simply because it has passed the tremendous brain power we find in the 26, or now 25, members of the cabinet.

October 10, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Cowan
I do not for one moment say that the cabinet is the government. In my opinion the government is the party to the right of the Speaker or, where there is a minority situation as in this case, the government is the majority of the House of Commons necessary to pass legislation.
I have in my hand a transcript of a talk by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) given on the C.B.C. television network at 10 p.m. on October 5, 1965, before the last election. In this talk the following statement was made:
The main reason for this election is that today there are major issues and problems facing Canada, and that in dealing with them the federal government-
Notice the reference to the federal government.
-can do the best possible job only if it has the support of a parliamentary majority-
What is the idea in separating the federal government and a parliamentary majority? Are they two separate and distinct things? In the 1965 election we went to the people looking for a parliamentary majority, but here the Prime Minister says that in dealing with the major issues and problems the federal government can do the best possible job only if it has the support of a parliamentary majority. Quite definitely, here we have the federal government being separated from parliament itself.
Then, speaking in Halifax on October 22, 1965 the Prime Minister stated:
Now, what we want to do in government is to have a government with a majority in the House of Commons-
If the cabinet is the government, then they cannot always have a majority in the House of Commons because there are only 25 or 26 of them and we know that is not a majority in a house of 265 members. Yet, we have the Prime Minister stating that what we want to do in government is to have a government with a majority in the House of Commons.
I agree with him that a government is a majority in the House of Commons, but I cannot agree with the practice which persists in referring to the cabinet as the government and which endeavours to make individual members simply ciphers of the will of the cabinet in the House of Commons. I apologize to the house as a whole, but interestingly I have in my hand a statement sent to me by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) having to do with the 1965 election. There is a very wholesome speech here by someone

brought in to speak at his nomination meeting. While there is a statement that it is a speech on behalf of the Minister of Labour, nowhere is the name of the speaker mentioned. I trust, therefore you will not ask me to identify who it was that spoke at the nomination meeting for the Minister of Labour in 1965; you would have to ask the Minister of Labour. In this speech the speaker said that the necessity for a strong central majority government is vital to Canada. There again, you have a man referring to the necessity for a strong central majority government.
The cabinet can never be a majority government. Therefore, what does it mean when we have what I call a cabinet and have a man going to Vancouver and asking for a majority government. An interesting comment in this regard is this. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) spoke on December 7, 1966 on the C.B.C. he started his address in this way:
Beginning next year, if parliament approves-
It is very, very seldom that I ever hear the members of the cabinet make any such remark, "if parliament approves". We hear in advance through the newspapers and radio from the cabinet exactly what parliament will approve, because if it does not approve the members who do not agree are rebels or heretics.

I stated that I wanted to refer to an item on page 560 of the blue book, amounting to $45 million in contingency estimates. When the Liberal party was sitting in the opposition on December 19, 1962 I held a seat somewhere close to that occupied by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg). At that time the leader of the Liberal opposition made this statement, as recorded at page 2834 of Hansard:
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made.
I have never heard a statement by a leader of an opposition party with which I agree more. I believe that is the right of any democratic parliament in any country in the world where such a system is followed. However, let me refer again to these contingency estimates in the blue book amounting to $45 million. I must recall the episode last November when a subterfuge was used whereby the cabinet took an amount of money passed for supplementary estimates and used it to pay civil servants salaries in order to dodge a non-confidence vote in this house. In order to indicate who runs the House of Commons let me remind you that I drove on November 10, 1966 from Toronto to Ottawa on the word of the government whip that my presence was necessary to carry a vote in order to get interim supply.
I sat here and listened to the Prime Minister outline what was to be done. As he did so, I became a little more burned up, particularly when I recalled his words that it was traditional and a fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they were collected and to approve expenditures before they were made. Surely, that is a fine mouthful of words when you are on the opposition side.
After it was announced in this house that the civil servants would be paid with interim supply money voted for other purposes I passed through the curtains to the members' lobby and grabbed a member of the cabinet, a lawyer. I said to him, What is the legal authority for this underhanded action on the
The Budget-Mr. Cowan part of the cabinet? This member said to me, "Ralph, I haven't the slightest idea; I was never consulted on the matter." I then grabbed another member of the cabinet who was passing by and asked him under what authority the civil service was being paid as a result of what had taken place in the House of Commons. He replied, I was never asked about the matter at all. About four days later, I spoke to another member of the cabinet who had not been present in this house on November 10, and said to him that it was too bad private members did not take their responsibility as easily or as lightly as members of the cabinet. I reminded him that he was not even in the house on November 10 when a vote was expected. This member of the cabinet replied to me, "R.B. I asked what they intended to do about paying the civil service and they told me what they intended to do, so I flew home"
Following that exchange I asked this member whom he meant by "they", and he just smiled. Let me suggest to you that "they" certainly are not a majority of this House of Commons. This is a certain group of people who decided to circumvent that vote in parliament by using interim supply funds voted for other purposes.
I am concerned about this $45 million contingency estimate in the blue book. It is still a fundamental right of parliament, as the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) said a long time ago, in 1962, to vote taxes before they are collected and approve expenditures before they are made. The public accounts committee of this house met last November and discussed this matter in detail. I have a copy of the report of that committee for Wednesday, March 1 covering its considerations of November 22 and 23. It is based pretty much on a statement prepared by the Auditor General of Canada, Mr. Henderson, in whom we all have utmost confidence. That committee discussed this matter in detail, following which it brought in its thirteenth report. Among the recommendations of that report following the evidence of Mr. Henderson the committee stated:
The committee discussed this statement on that date and questioned the Secretary of the Treasury Board who provided the members with additional helpful information on the subject. This discussion brought out clearly both the significance and importance of parliament's control of public funds and the need for continued vigilance on the part of all members of the house to ensure that the control is effectively and properly exercised.
The committee is of the opinion that there is a weakening of parliamentary control when parliament is unable to take the time to examine in detail the amounts being requested as interim

It considers it unfortunate that the parliamentary rules do not provide for immediate consideration of the estimates after they are presented to the house so that the proposed spending can be approved and interim supply would not be required so extensively. It feels that the rules could and should be changed in this regard in order not only to strengthen parliamentary control of public funds but to give the executive the clear mandate it deserves in the discharge of its heavy responsibilities.
The committee submits the following recommendations designed to strengthen parliamentary control of public expenditures in the future:

If a change like this were to be made, then the finance contingencies vote could be returned to its original concept, namely that of a small fund to be retained for unexpected and unforeseen items.
I believe we are experiencing a mockery of democracy as long as we withhold from the parliament of Canada the opportunity of passing on these estimates for interim supply, if it is necessary to have interim supply, because we are being asked to vote in this case $45 million, and were asked to vote not long ago $110 million to the contingency fund. [DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
While I am saying, Mr. Speaker, that we in Canada have much to be grateful for, it is obvious that we are facing critical financial and economic problems. Ever since we resumed our session two weeks ago the major burden of the debate has rotated around such subjects as the housing crisis and inflation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) now adds another interesting, ambiguous phrase by referring to "the necessity for managing prosperity".
I am not going to deal, Mr. Speaker, with these all too obvious difficulties that have been referred to by many members in the course of the budget debate. However, I am going to suggest that one of the main reasons the government finds itself in a difficult and complex financial situation at the present time is its tendency to take as gospel truth its own propaganda. It has begun to believe in its own inspired publicity releases, and over the past few years that the Liberal party has been in power this tendency has created a psychological atmosphere which is becoming increasingly difficult to control.


It was interesting to listen to the impassioned plea of the Minister of Finance as he attempted to dampen down the fires of inflation that have been kindled by this psychological propaganda campaign. Obviously the President of the Treasury Board and Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) does not accept the advice of the Minister of Finance, because this afternoon he made a speech which indicated he was still of the opinion that there is nothing critically wrong with the state of the economy in Canada.
It is also of interest, Mr. Speaker, that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon), the former minister of finance, was the first to reject publicly the appeal of the present Minister of Finance for voluntary restraint. He has been the perennial optimist of the Liberal government and Liberal cabinet, and in his speech the other evening he saw nothing about which to be unduly worried. He said everything would straighten itself out in due course if we would all refrain from rocking the boat.
This is an indication, Mr. Speaker, of the difficulties the Minister of Finance is experiencing in controlling the spending habits of his own colleagues in the cabinet, and it accounts for the runaway inflation from which Canada has been suffering during the past two or three years.
In his comments this afternoon the Minister of National Revenue sought to compare the wonderful state of the economy with the rather unhappy state of affairs that existed, say, six, seven or eight years ago when another party was in power. This is the basis for the propaganda which has led the present government into the slough of despond in which it finds itself at the moment.
I should like to take the opportunity, once and for all, to give the lie to this persistent propaganda that at the beginning of the sixties things were going to the dogs in fiscal and monetary terms but that now we are headed into the promised land of prosperity; that, to use the phrase of the Minister of Finance once again, all we have to do is to manage our continuing Liberal prosperity.
I like to read the speeches of ministers from time to time, Mr. Speaker, especially those that are delivered beyond the shores of Canada, because sometimes a non-partisan and objective viewpoint is expressed of the sort that is not often heard when a minister speaks in this country. The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale President of the Privy Council and the Minister of National Revenue during this debate have turned aside from the appeal of the Minister of Finance for restraint within the government.
There is a tendency, too, to blame the provinces. I want to deal with this aspect of the government's interpretation of the current economic crisis for a few moments. When the government resumed office in 1963, part of its propaganda barrage was that the spirit of co-operative federalism would reign supreme in the administration of Canadian affairs at all levels. This was wise, because with our divided jurisdictions and our political and economic structure we can deal with national economic and fiscal policies successfully only by the closest possible inter governmental co-operation. It is distressing to see the current trend; now that the government is in trouble it tries to tie the can to the tail of the provincial cat.
I shall deal with one instance to show what the government currently is doing. In the manpower area, for example, we have recently seen a thoroughgoing revision of the functions of the unemployment insurance commission and national employment service; the name of the organization has been changed to the department of manpower. Ottawa has moved wholesale into this area on the strength of the constitutional amendment which was necessary to set up the unemployment insurance commission. All these revisions entail, it seems to me, a propaganda approach. The term "manpower" in this area of economic activity is popular among social scientists today and the government has applied it to its revamped national employment service. I will not say whether that is wise or unwise, but I do say that in moving wholesale into this area the effect on the government's retraining program has been disturbing. Some aspect of this has already been discussed and there will be more discussion along these lines as the current year takes shape.
In the medicare field, several speakers have referred to the urgent necessity for further conferences and consultations between Ottawa and the provincial governments. Medicare is an important new development in the social welfare and health field. This brings us to something that has been referred to several times in the debate, the necessity of emphasing priorities of expenditure. The Minister of Finance and the President of the Privy Council, through their responses to
2962	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale suggestions from opposition spokesmen, seem to think that we are against medicare. That is a propaganda line and is patently false. One could call it plain, cheap politics with respect to this important health measure. We are asking for further consultation because the provinces are unhappy with the fiscal demands that will be placed on them by this arbitrarily imposed federal initiative. They object not only to the fiscal demands but also to the inadequacy of the federal government's proposed program. This leads one to comment on the whole approach of the Liberal government to the social welfare and health field.
There has been complete lack of planning and rationalization of our health and welfare programs to meet the demands of these important areas of human activity. The government's emphasis is on what one might call the welfare state, a concept that is rapidly becoming outmoded in the light of experience of countries which have gone holus-bolus for the welfare state, such as the United Kingdom and, to a lesser extent, Sweden, with its great social democratic experiment.
The provinces are not demanding cradle to the grave welfare, which takes care of one whether one needs it or not. The provinces are providing realistic leadership here. They are asking for priorities. The implication of priorities is that we shall develop a social program that will provide assistance where it is needed and help Canadians everywhere to deal with handicaps, whether they are educational, fiscal or physical, that they may fulfil themselves to their maximum advantage within a free society. Before we become embroiled in a medicare scheme which does not come to grips with the fundamental and broader needs of health care in today's Canadian society, the federal government would be well advised to call together the provinces and to listen carefully to what they are saying on these matters.
The Prime Minister has entered this debate. Defending the charge that the federal government has been unwisely lavish in its expenditure of public funds, he said that the provinces are in precisely the same position and are just as guilty as Ottawa in making unnecessary expenditures.
I shall not defend the provinces; I am not familiar with what has happened in every province, but I can speak for my own province, Manitoba, which had a change of government in 1958. The government of that year replaced one which had been continuously in office since 1922. The proud boast of the old government had been that it had the

The obvious answer is that the level of services provided was also the lowest. It happened to be a Liberal provincial regime, and if recent provincial expenditures in that province have increased at substantial rates in the past it is because of the need to remedy the long years of neglect particularly in the area of education. Manitoba has made education its number one priority, a position taken by a number of other provinces which realise that in order to make it possible for human resources to be used with maximum effect people must be provided with the schooling that is necessary.
Over the weekend we were given an example of what is happening in Manitoba and in other provinces in Canada which have had to take a lead in meeting the rapidly growing need for higher education. Over the weekend Brandon College formally assumed university status. Among the special events which took place was the conferring upon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) of an honorary doctorate. So, from this point onward the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre can be addressed as "Doctor".
As to this tendency to criticize provincial authorities, I wish to refer to another matter in which I have taken a close interest during the past several years, the whole subject of recreational park development. It was hoped in 1962 that the government would meet the rapidly increasing demand for recreational services for our urbanized society. It was hoped that Ottawa would seize the initiative in promoting an effective recreational parks development program. Each year since then discussions have been held on the subject, promises have been made and we have been told that some scheme or another was just around the corner. Nothing materialized and the provinces have at last got tired of waiting for federal initiative, with the result that right across the country they are moving into this area of park development, something which involves the expenditure of considerable sums of money. I think this is an area which accounts in a substantial measure for at least some of the expenditures by provincial government to which the Prime Minister referred.
The same applies to the roads to resources program, another co-operative federal scheme which has been discontinued by the present government. Roads are basic to development
