In any event, I put the question to the hon. Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) ten days ago. The hon. minister did not know and a civil servant who was seated up in the gallery sent her the note I have here, in which he said bluntly:

Minister: Re Caouette question on C.B.C. French services to B.C., the situation is:
Radio-an application for establishment of a French language F. M. station in Vancouver has been approved and the station is expected to be on air November 1.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: My hon. friend from Vancouver East asks me why. I say to help him to understand French in Vancouver when he is there.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: I spend a lot of time in Ottawa.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Maybe you would prefer to be in China. You have only to go if you want. Nobody stops you from going. The note continues:
T.V.-in long-range plans but nothing definite at this stage.
2S64	COMMONS DEBATES	October 10, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
I see my hon. friend from York-Humber applauding because apparently it will take another decade, or two decades, before they get t.v. in French in Vancouver.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Why in French, man?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Why an English T.V. station in my own district? Tell me why?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is beyond my understanding when I see narrow-minded people cause prejudice to unity and understanding among Canadians. As for me, I was happy to learn the English language when nothing whatsoever compelled me to do so.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Indeed, I learned that language.
We are glad we have English radio and television stations in the cities of Quebec and Trois-Rivieres, because we are aware that the English-speaking Canadians of Quebec enjoy, in our province, the same rights as we do.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: I declare, Mr. Speaker, that I should enjoy the same rights in British Columbia, in Saskatchewan, in Alberta, in Manitoba-

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: But the English are paying for French T.V.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: And the French are paying part of your salary here in Ottawa.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Listen to that, Mr. Speaker. I have just been told that Vancouver taxpayers will be paying for that.
Mr. Speaker, over the weekend, we had our convention of the Ralliement Creditiste in Quebec. Today, I read an article in La Presse written by a newspaperman who attended the convention. Just to show you to what extent a newspaper man can be-possibly not dishonest-but lost in the clouds, like certain leaders we have in province of Quebec, I shall read what he wrote:
Mr. Caouette's concept on the constitution is well known. Canada should continue to exist as is. There is only one country and two cultures that should be officially recognized.
[Mr. Caouette.}
That is not at all what I said. So, I should like to repeat here in the house what I said at the convention, so that it will be recorded in Hansard and my friends for York-Humber and Vancouver (Messrs. Cowan and Winch) will know exactly what my personal convictions are and know also the convictions of the group I represent in the house and those of all our partisans in the province.
Mr. Speaker, there are not ten Canadas, according to the whims of wishes of the provinces. There are not five Canadas. There is but one country, called Canada, from Newfoundland to Vancouver. I hope my friend, over here, has understood me.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: One Canada?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: One Canada. Now that my hon. friend agrees with me, he will be willing to pay taxes for a French T.V. station in Vancouver.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: No "two nations."

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
No two nations, no special
privileges.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: One Canada.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Yes, and respect between all the others existing in Canada. Now, let me finish my statement.

One Canada, with the various cultures it is made of. Not two cultures, but several cultures! And I know what I am talking about!
At home, in Rouyn-Noranda, we have Ukrainians, Poles, Italians, Russians, Finns, Yugoslavs, Tchecoslovakians. We have about every culture, and mind you, they each have their own association. Each group has its association in our area. Every year these various groups have their celebrations, and we are glad and happy to see, for instance, the Ukrainians celebrate their feast. We attend their folk dances and their sing-songs. We see the Poles and the Germans performing theirs. And two years ago, during a trip to Winnipeg, I noted the same thing in that area. These Ukrainian, Polish, Italian and German people are neither French Canadians nor English Canadians, but they are still Canadians, and I am convinced of their cultural contribution to Canada.
I would like to continue my speech. Canada is one country. We should not be afraid to
Ociober 10, 1967

say it. The proponents of the two-nation concept, three nations, one and one fourth nation, who do not know the meaning of the word "nation", have said: We are in favour of two nations. What does this mean? This means "two founding people". This is not what "nation" implies. A nation, to my mind, is all the citizens of a same country. Here, in Canada, we have citizens of various origins, living in a country called Canada.
Mr. Speaker, several cultures, two official languages. Two official languages-
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: There is only one official language.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Two official languages. [English]

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: The other is permissive.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Your English in my province is permissive and this is because we want to respect you. We are giving you permission to speak your language in our province.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
One official language- French.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Yorlt-Humber (Mr. Cowan) is more of a separatist than the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), in that case.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Two official languages-

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: One.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: -because our country was in fact built by two different ethnic groups, two different cultures. The Ukrainians, the Poles, the Italians, the Germans, the Russians and the Slavs who come to Canada do not refuse to learn English or French, nor to accept these two as the official languages of the whole country, not only of Quebec. No, they are official in the whole of Canada.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
When our forbears discovered Canada, they did not discover Toronto, Montreal or Quebec city only, they discovered the whole of Canada, and some of our people live in western Canada, just as there are Anglo-Saxons in Quebec. It is strange that, in the
The Budget-Mr. Caouette province of Quebec, we do not hear Anglo-Saxons complain about the way they are treated.
I will now complete my remarks, I will explain my position. National unity, according to the member for York-Humber, would consist in speaking only one language in Canada. In my opinion, national unity is something else. When the member for York-Humber treats French-speaking Canadians in Ontario and elsewhere in Canada as we treat the English-speaking minority in Quebec, then we will have national unity.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: That does not mean that the hon. member must learn French, no. There are in Quebec English-speaking people who have always refused to learn French; that is their business. However, is not my very good friend, who is in favour of the monarchy, a little ashamed when he hears Her Majesty the Queen of England speak French practically as well as we do?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: There is not a single Prime Minister of Great Britain who does not speak French. The hon. member for York-Humber is still one of those Orangemen from Toronto who have always refused to learn anything but English.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow me a question?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that the grandfather of the hon. member for York-Humber who is buried in a Trois-Rivieres cemetery spoke French?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: His children turned out scamps.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) for letting me know. It is unfortunate that the grandson did not follow in his grandfather's footsteps.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once more in a serious vein, I feel that when Canadians, from coast to coast, understand not only the necessity but the urgency of recognizing the two official languages right across Canada, we
2966	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Caouette will then help all our fellow-citizens, regardless of their origin; we will then respect the very basis of confederation, the very basis of the agreement between French-speaking and English-speaking citizens.
Then, Mr. Speaker, a lot of things will be settled, many problems solved. But as long as there are narrow-minded people on both sides-and there are some also among French Canadians, namely Pierre Bourgault of the R.I.N.-it will be more difficult. I watched Pierre Bourgault on television last night. As of yesterday, he is against terrorism; the day before, he was ready to sink ships going through the St. Lawrence seaway. One day, he is a terrorist, the day after, he is not.
This is to show you, Mr. Speaker, that this matter is very important. But it will be settled much more easily after the economic problem is geared to present needs and solved so as to meet the requirements of all Canadians.
And here is a clipping from La Presse where the former minister of justice of Quebec, Mr. Claude Wagner says:
Convinced that, on the whole, the population of Quebec does not care a hoot about the constitutional crisis and that the citizens of Quebec, according to him, mostly want "bread, butter, security, order and justice", Mr. Wagner stated that the Quebec political elite should come to its senses and deal with the problems facing Quebec.
And not only Quebec, but all over. Further on, he speaks of the famous war on poverty that seems to be forgotten everywhere.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that we have been hearing about war on poverty in parliament for some time. Themes have been brought forward, yes, but no solution. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) said on October 2, as reported on page 2730 of Hansard:
But I decided it really was not necessary because I remember with what wholehearted enthusiasm the members of the official opposition urged us to spend hundreds of millions of dollars in excess of what we have.
When I hear the Minister of Finance or his assistant talk to us about "spending money in excess of what we have" I wonder what are our means? The means given to us by Washington? The financial or physical means at our disposal for the development of our country? Do we have the physical means necessary for development in the field of housing construction, food prices, the increase of agricultural production and the establishment of secondary industries in Canada, or

DEBATES	October 10, 1967
are we only to take into account our financial resources? I understand that the minister, or the government, has to ask New York for the financial permission to develop anything in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, all this is very annoying. So far as financial means are concerned, it is more than a simple question of "means", for we are asked for interest which we pay without paying off the capital. We, members of the Ralliement Creditiste, still maintain that whatever may be accomplished physically in Canada could and should be financed through the Bank of Canada. I see that my hon. friend from Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) finds that funny. In fact, he was telling me a while ago that we agree as to the constitutional problem right up to the point concerning the Bank of Canada.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Now, merely to include the Bank of Canada in the constitutional debate would allow the bank to finance our economy and to wage war efficiently against poverty. Then, other constitutional problems would be easily solved, since no one is more interested than our people in seeing an improvement in the economic climate.
And when we hear-

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: It would be a good thing to abolish election funds.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
This would be a step in the right direction, to abolish election funds, so as to save more money to fight poverty. However, Mr. Speaker, complaints are being heard today from certain people, especially from Quebec, who decry Ottawa: Ottawa steps on the provinces' toes; if things go wrong, it is Ottawa's fault; if things are going wrong in Quebec, it is because of Ottawa.
I have here a table showing the various taxes levied in the ten Canadian provinces. This chart was prepared by Mr. Henri Bel-lehumeur of Rouyn, after he had inquired from every province about sales taxes, taxes on meals, hotel rooms, soft drinks, hard liquor, telecommunications, tobacco, cigarettes, and gasoline.
In Quebec, it is 8 per cent across the board. Nobody can say it was Ottawa who imposed the 8 per cent tax; or the 48-cent tax on cartons of cigarettes; or the 16-cent tax on gasoline. If we compare this situation with that prevailing in Alberta who has only 2 million inhabitants, we find that there are no such taxes except for a 12-cent tax on gasoline. In fact, meals, hotel rooms, soft drinks, drinks in
October 10, 19G7

general, beer, telecommunications, tobacco and cigarette cartons are not taxed at all.
Mr. Speaker, Alberta is also part of our country of Canada, and so is British Columbia. In Ontario, they also have a 5 per cent sales tax, but no tax on hotel rooms, and only 20 cents tax on a carton of cigarettes. Those are provinces of Canada. Those taxes were not imposed by Ottawa^ the decision was entirely theirs, and in Quebec on top of all that we have a provincial income tax.
I understand that equalization payments are made by Ottawa to offset the tax levied by Quebec; I agree. But the Canadian citizen, Mr. Speaker is paying double tax, and this is not Ottawa's fault. Ottawa should not always be blamed. Everyone should start by taking his responsibilities in his own province.
I feel that if Quebec is now the most heavily taxed province, confederation is not to blame but the governments we elected. That is where the responsibility lies.
There is no doubt that Ottawa is not blame-meless and must be brought back to reason but the provinces must assume their responsibilities. That is where we stand. When the provinces get together with Ottawa, instead of talking only about the right to relieve the people of their money, about taxation, as we say, to use words that everyone does not understand all the time, they should discuss monetary reforms, basic reforms and say, like the famous general who one day came to Canada or the province of Quebec: Let us go to the heart of things. Let us do it and we will see that the heart of the matter is money.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), who is in his seat, would be happy if he did not have any monetary problem in his department. But he forgets about the monetary problem; he looks only at the fiscal problem, as is done in all departments, especially in the Department of Finance, that is the right to levy taxes.
If the provinces do not like it, all they have to do is increase taxes. It is true that they have the right to do it. But if Ottawa does not reduce taxes in proportion to the increases levied in the provinces, the Canadian people, the worker, the farmer, the white-collar worker will be unable to pay more. Let us go at the bottom of things, but let us do it. It is not only a matter of speaking French or English, it is a matter of living in one's country and everybody knows that Canada is one of the richest countries in the world. Now, it is unthinkable to see poverty in the midst of
The Budget-Mr. Olson plenty. Let us open or break down the doors of poverty to enable abundance to meet the needs of every Canadian citizen and we will then attain national unity.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question I should like to ask is, irrespective of the treaty with Paris of 1763; irrespective of the ethnic, cultural and language groups that make up Canada, would the hon. member following his statement stand up and say that he agrees with the unity of Canada, that he is a Canadian and proud of it?

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, probably I should not bother to answer such a silly question. However, I should like to say that I am not living in 1763 and I am not considering what happened prior to that date. I do know one thing. Our confederation was founded in 1867. Since that time I am convinced that Canadians of all extractions recognize the right of bilingualism in our country, namely the French and English languages. That is the wish of the people.

maintopic: A. R. MITCHELL DEPUTY CITY CLERK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the very few minutes we have left before the vote is called tonight I should like to deal briefly with two subjects, the wheat and flour markets and the difficulty in respect of the administration of transportation policy in Canada. Before doing so, let me say that having listened to the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), and I happen to be a member from an area some distance from here in western Canada, I find myself in a very large measure of agreement in respect of many of the things he has advanced which would contribute to the national unity of Canada today.
We are concerned about what seems to be some uncertainty in the international wheat and flour markets today. The Canadian wheat board ought to be granted additional authority to meet the competition that exists in these international markets. We can look back and find case after case where the selling agencies for wheat and flour in the United States have undertaken massive campaigns, particularly in the Orient, to teach and convince the bakers in that part of the world the value of using different blends of flour containing higher percentages of United States winter wheat.
This kind of competition is very difficult to meet and I believe that if the Canadian wheat board is to be confined only to meeting

October 10, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Olson competition so tar as price is concerned this policy will prove even more expensive than some of those undertakings required to meet other kinds of salesmanship in this area. I have before me a Searle grain company report of about two years ago which suggests that a concerted effort was made by wheat selling agencies in the United States to hold what would amount to almost seminars or training programs in Japan in order to demonstrate that flour milled from about 50 per cent United States hard wheat and 50 per cent spring wheat could result in products equal to or superior to those using 100 per cent spring wheat. That refers, of course, to Canadian wheat.
I am aware of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) is now in Japan attempting to restore and expand some of the markets we have held over the years. I believe we must go a little further than that to meet this other kind of competition by sending representatives from our industry to make sure that the Japanese bakers are cognizant of the value of a very high level of Canadian wheat in their flour.
The other point I want to make is that we should not separate the wheat and flour markets because they are one and the same thing as far as the Canadian producer of wheat is concerned. Any time we sell flour from Canada it is a foregone conclusion that it is made completely from Canadian wheat. During the years from 1957 to 1962 there was a steady decline in the export of flour from Canada to the Orient. In 1956 we exported to that part of the world something over 4 million hundredweight of flour. By 1962 this amount had dropped to slightly over 2 million hundredweight. This diminishing market for flour in the Orient is damaging what used to be one of the largest industries in Canada, namely the production of high grade flour from Canadian wheat.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I hope that the minister's efforts in the Orient will be successful and will be followed up by experts who will enlarge this training program, if you want to call it that, of using high levels of Canadian wheat and flour in the bread-making industries of these countries.
There appear to be only four or five minutes left to me, Mr. Speaker. I now wish to turn the attention of the house to a matter that is of extreme importance to us in Canada. I refer to the question of transportation. We know that at the present time a

government agency, in other words the Canadian Transportation Commission, is in the process of taking over from the Board of Transport Commissioners. I suppose it is too early to be critical of what the transportation commission is doing in applying the provisions laid down by parliament this year in the new transportation bill. However, there are a great many difficulties developing in the railway industry in the transition period.
My purpose tonight is to urge the new transportation commission to get under way and set up as quickly as possible all the facilities they need so that the provisions of those sections that were put into the transportation act will be available to the shippers. It is extremely important that the costing department of the transportation commission be set up and made functional at once, because the provisions of section 336, for example, and section 16 of that act, wherein a shipper has recourse to the transportation commission, cannot be applied until we have accurate and acceptable costing methods, techniques, formulae, and so on. This has not been done to this time.
It may be rather early to be critical of the new commission, but I know that a large number of shippers in western Canada today are suffering because they have no recourse in respect of the rate adjustments which the railways are making. It will be a very formidable task for whoever first appears before the new transportation commission to plead his case against discrimination and unjust rates. Therefore, we need these facilities to be made available to shippers at the earliest possible moment.
I hope, in closing, Mr. Speaker, that the transportation commission will have all these facilities operative in the very near future so that what the house intended to be available to the shippers of Canada will in fact be available without any great time loss.
